He said: "Margaret. I was in the room when Walter declined. I was in the room when he wrote the paper on supportive therapy in 2009. I have known this man since I was 24 years old and I could not give him one thing to hold onto."

"And I could have. If any of us had looked one inch outside the textbook, we could have handed him something to do every morning. He sat in a chair waiting for three months because we all read the same book and none of us questioned it."

"Margaret. Walter died with nothing in his hands but a plan that told him to wait. And I am the doctor who was supposed to be his second opinion."

I had to put the phone down.

I sat at the kitchen table for a long time after he hung up.

Because if Marcus at Cleveland Clinic — one of the top three kidney doctors in the country — did not give Walter a lever, and Marcus needed one himself, then nobody currently practising nephrology in this country is handing their patients one.

And neither is anyone they are treating giving it to themselves.

Then there was my son-in-law in Boston.

46, two young kids, works ninety-hour weeks at a hedge fund. His last annual had come back with "mildly reduced kidney function, nothing to worry about, keep an eye on it."

He had been waking in the night and dragging through his afternoons for over a year, which his doctor had brushed off as "probably stress."

I sent him a box before he asked. My daughter told him it was not a request.

He started drinking it in early April. By late June the night waking had eased and the afternoon fog had lifted.

He told me on the phone that he had not realised how long he had been dragging until he wasn't.

His most recent annual came back with his kidney number no longer moving in the direction it had been going.

Then there was my neighbour Ellen.

Her husband had declined the same way Walter did, four months before Walter. Two widows on the same block.

She started drinking it two days after I told her.

She said it was the first time since her husband died that she felt like she was doing something for herself in the morning instead of just waiting for her own next appointment.

I told my sister in Michigan. I told Walter's brother in Denver. I told the three women in my Wednesday book club whose husbands had "borderline" numbers.

I told Marcus to tell his own residents at Cleveland Clinic, quietly, off the record, if he could.

I have lost count of the number of boxes I have sent. My daughter has stopped asking me to keep the receipts.

I should be grateful. Every one of these people has something to do every morning now. Their wives are not going to sit where I am sitting feeling like they never got to try.

But this is not gratitude I am feeling.

What I am feeling, every time somebody tells me their number held, is that I spent 38 years in a house with the most respected kidney doctor in the state and neither of us thought to look outside the book he was handed for one small thing he could do.

I had a laptop. I had time.

Any Sunday afternoon in the last ten years I could have sat next to Walter at this table and asked him one question about a daily lever.

I did not. He did not. And he sat in a chair waiting until there was nothing left to do.

Marcus has something to hold onto because a widow with too much time and a laptop finally asked the question nobody asked while my husband was alive.

And that is why I am writing this to you.

Because you still have time.

Your husband is still alive. Your brother is still alive. Your father is still alive.

The question I did not ask until it was too late — you can ask it tonight.

I am not a doctor. I am not a scientist. I am not selling anything and I do not get a penny from any of this.

I am a 61-year-old widow sitting in my husband's chair at 2 in the morning because I cannot sleep and I cannot stop thinking about my son-in-law in Boston and the mornings he struggled through that his doctor said were probably stress and how many other people are sitting in a chair every three months waiting for a verdict tonight and how many of them have wives who are reading things exactly like this and deciding whether or not to trust them.

Here is what I know because I lived it.

The textbook watches the numbers. It hands you nothing to do. Walter's plan was all subtraction and all waiting.

Detox tea is a diuretic with a marketing word on the box.

Capsule CoQ10 is the right idea in the wrong form. Most of the dose never gets where it needs to go.

The two things that actually let a person watching their kidney numbers stop feeling helpless are a daily lever that gently supports healthy blood pressure and the agency of a ritual you can keep every morning.

The outpatient plan gives neither. It watches, it subtracts, and it waits.

Walter followed the best plan any doctor in America could give him and he sat in a chair waiting for three months while nobody handed him one thing to do.

I still watched the numbers. But I was no longer empty-handed.

I wish somebody had told us before May 22nd.

Before he ran his own labs at 6 AM. Before he sat at the kitchen table with the printout in his hand and told me we had a problem.

Before the 162 days of egg whites and white toast. Before the seven bottles lined up on the shelf above the coffee maker.

Before November 16th at 4:43 AM.

I cannot go back. Walter cannot come back. His white coat is still on the back of the bedroom door and it is going to stay there.

But you can still go forward.

Your husband can. Your brother can. Your father can. You can.

Everything I have told you about PiPi Tea — the whole hibiscus flower, the high-altitude growing, the hand-picking, the organic sourcing, the intact flower instead of ground dust — you can see for yourself right now.

This is the tea Marcus keeps on his desk at Cleveland Clinic. This is the tea my son-in-law in Boston drinks every morning.

This is the tea I ordered five boxes of the week I found the Portland doctor's post.

A lever for the pressure. A hand on the wheel. That is the whole answer.

I want you to look at it. Not for me. For whoever you would leave behind.

I listened to my dead husband's voicemail for the 47th time this morning while I sat in my car in the Kroger parking lot with the engine off.

"Hey Janie, it's me, traffic's a mess on 64, I'm gonna be late, don't hold dinner, love you, bye."

11 seconds long. 11 seconds. I have it memorized down to the breath he takes between "love you" and "bye." There's a tiny pause there, like he was about to say something else and didn't. I've spent two years wondering what he was about to say.

Frank died on October 11th, 2023. Massive heart attack at his desk at the Charleston Gazette-Mail, where he'd been a sports editor for 31 years. He was 61. He'd left me that voicemail on April 3rd of that same year. Six months and 8 days before.

I save it. I move it from one phone to the next. The Verizon guy who set up my new iPhone last December asked me if I needed help transferring anything and I said yes, my voicemails, all of them, and he looked at me funny because nobody saves voicemails anymore, but he did it, and I gave him a $20 tip because he didn't ask why.

My name is Janet. Everyone calls me Janie. I'm 58 years old. I live in a brick split-level on the south end of Charleston, West Virginia, the kind of street where the dogwoods come in pink along both curbs in April and where everyone knows whose Subaru is whose. Frank and I bought the house in 1997 when our son Eli was 4. Eli is 33 now, lives in Pittsburgh, calls me every Sunday at 6:30 PM whether I pick up or not.

I haven't checked my blood pressure since the funeral.

I have one of those little arm cuffs in the linen closet, on the second shelf, behind the towels Frank's mother gave us in 1995. It still has the receipt taped to the side because Frank refused to throw away the receipt on anything that cost more than $40. The cuff was $52 from CVS. He bought it after his cardiologist Dr. Marsh told him he needed to start tracking his numbers at home, and Frank, being Frank, came home with one for each of us, because he said if we were going to do something we were going to do it together.

He took his every morning at 6:14 AM, sitting at the kitchen table in his blue plaid robe, before the coffee was even done. He wrote the numbers in a yellow legal pad with the date and a little notation if he'd slept bad or eaten something salty. The legal pad is still in the kitchen drawer. I haven't opened it. I can't.

I haven't taken mine since the morning of October 12th, 2023. Which was the morning after Frank died. I sat at the table by myself and put the cuff on and watched the number come up and then I took the whole machine and put it in the linen closet behind the towels and I haven't touched it since.

The number was 168 over 102, if you're wondering.

I am not stupid. I know what 168 over 102 means. I worked as the office manager at a pediatric practice for 24 years before I retired in 2022. I sat across the desk from Dr. Rinaldi for nearly a quarter century, and I know what a blood pressure reading is supposed to look like, and I know what one looks like when it isn't.

But I also know what grief is. And grief, the kind that comes for a woman who lost her husband suddenly at 61 with no warning, is the kind that says: I will deal with my body later. Frank would have wanted you to.

body:
I listened to my dead husband's voicemail for the 47th time this morning while I sat in my car in the Kroger parking lot with the engine off.

"Hey Janie, it's me, traffic's a mess on 64, I'm gonna be late, don't hold dinner, love you, bye."

11 seconds long. 11 seconds. I have it memorized down to the breath he takes between "love you" and "bye." There's a tiny pause there, like he was about to say something else and didn't. I've spent two years wondering what he was about to say.

Frank died on October 11th, 2023. Massive heart attack at his desk at the Charleston Gazette-Mail, where he'd been a sports editor for 31 years. He was 61. He'd left me that voicemail on April 3rd of that same year. Six months and 8 days before.

I save it. I move it from one phone to the next. The Verizon guy who set up my new iPhone last December asked me if I needed help transferring anything and I said yes, my voicemails, all of them, and he looked at me funny because nobody saves voicemails anymore, but he did it, and I gave him a $20 tip because he didn't ask why.

My name is Janet. Everyone calls me Janie. I'm 58 years old. I live in a brick split-level on the south end of Charleston, West Virginia, the kind of street where the dogwoods come in pink along both curbs in April and where everyone knows whose Subaru is whose. Frank and I bought the house in 1997 when our son Eli was 4. Eli is 33 now, lives in Pittsburgh, calls me every Sunday at 6:30 PM whether I pick up or not.

I haven't checked my blood pressure since the funeral.

I have one of those little arm cuffs in the linen closet, on the second shelf, behind the towels Frank's mother gave us in 1995. It still has the receipt taped to the side because Frank refused to throw away the receipt on anything that cost more than $40. The cuff was $52 from CVS. He bought it after his cardiologist Dr. Marsh told him he needed to start tracking his numbers at home, and Frank, being Frank, came home with one for each of us, because he said if we were going to do something we were going to do it together.

He took his every morning at 6:14 AM, sitting at the kitchen table in his blue plaid robe, before the coffee was even done. He wrote the numbers in a yellow legal pad with the date and a little notation if he'd slept bad or eaten something salty. The legal pad is still in the kitchen drawer. I haven't opened it. I can't.

I haven't taken mine since the morning of October 12th, 2023. Which was the morning after Frank died. I sat at the table by myself and put the cuff on and watched the number come up and then I took the whole machine and put it in the linen closet behind the towels and I haven't touched it since.

The number was 168 over 102, if you're wondering.

I am not stupid. I know what 168 over 102 means. I worked as the office manager at a pediatric practice for 24 years before I retired in 2022. I sat across the desk from Dr. Rinaldi for nearly a quarter century, and I know what a blood pressure reading is supposed to look like, and I know what one looks like when it isn't.

But I also know what grief is. And grief, the kind that comes for a woman who lost her husband suddenly at 61 with no warning, is the kind that says: I will deal with my body later. I will get through Thanksgiving first. I will get through Christmas. I will get through his birthday. I will get through our anniversary. I will get through the one year mark. I will get through the two year mark.

And the years go by and you don't deal with it.

And every morning you wake up and your head feels heavy and your face feels hot when you stand up too fast and you tell yourself it's because you didn't sleep well, or because you're dehydrated, or because the weather changed, or because you had two glasses of wine with Carol on Thursday night. You tell yourself anything except the thing.

The thing is, my husband died of his heart at 61. And I am a 58-year-old woman whose blood pressure was 168 over 102 the morning after he died and who has not checked it in two years and three months.

Carol Whitfield has been my best friend since 1996. She lives 4 streets over on Ridgeway Drive in a yellow Cape Cod with a flagstone path. She and her husband Dr. Marsh, the same Dr. Marsh who'd been Frank's cardiologist, used to come over for cards every other Friday. Dr. Marsh is 64 now, retired in 2024 from his practice but still consults two days a week at CAMC. He was the one who pronounced Frank at the hospital. He drove me home in his own car. He sat at my kitchen table at 9:47 PM that night and didn't say anything for 23 minutes, just sat there with his hand on my hand, and then he said, "Janie, the man loved you to pieces. He talked about you like a boy."

I haven't been able to look him in the eye since.

Not because of anything he did. Because of what he knows.

He knows Frank's numbers. He has them in a file somewhere. He knows what Frank's blood pressure was running in those last 6 months. He knows what mine was the only time I let him take it, at Carol's 55th birthday party in 2022, when he had one of those wrist cuffs out and was making people guess theirs as a joke. Mine was 154 over 96 with a glass of pinot grigio in my hand. He'd raised an eyebrow at me. Said, "Janie, when are you coming in?" I'd laughed and walked into the kitchen for more cheese.

A year and a half later he was driving me home from the hospital where my husband had died.

He has tried to talk to me three times in the last two years. At Frank's memorial. At Eli's wedding in May of 2024. Standing in line at the deli counter at Capitol Market last September. Each time I have made my voice bright and said "I am doing fine, doctor, you take care now," and walked away.

Last Thursday he showed up at my front door at 4:47 PM with a Pyrex casserole dish covered in tinfoil.

Carol was at her sister's in Roanoke. He was alone. He had the casserole in both hands and a folder under his arm.

I stared at him through the storm door for a long second.

"Carol made too much lasagna," he said. "She said you'd take the leftovers off our hands if I begged."

That is a lie. Carol does not over-make lasagna. Carol portions everything in advance because she ran the church food pantry for 11 years. Dr. Marsh knew I knew it was a lie. He held the casserole up a little higher and said, "Can I come in, Janie."

I let him in.

He set the lasagna on the kitchen counter, on the exact spot where Frank used to set the mail on Tuesdays. Then he sat down at the kitchen table without being asked, in Frank's chair, and put his hands flat on the placemat, and looked at me, and said:

"Janie, you haven't been in to see anyone in two years. I know because I have a friend at every cardiology practice in Charleston and I asked. I'm not here as your doctor. I'm here as Frank's friend. And I cannot watch this happen twice."

I didn't say anything.

He opened the folder.

In it was a single piece of paper. A photocopy of Frank's last in-office blood pressure reading from August 14th, 2023. 8 weeks before he died.

158 over 96. With a little note in Dr. Marsh's handwriting in the margin: "FU 3 mo. discuss adjustment."

He never made it to the follow-up.

Then he said the thing that broke me a second time.

He said: "Frank would have taken it, Janie. If he'd known. He was that kind of man. He would have read the same articles I read and he would have ordered a bottle for both of you. You both would have been on it for two years by now."

I looked at the bottle on the table next to the paper that said 158 over 96.

I think you can guess what I did.

I want to slow down here and tell you what I learned in the next 4 days, because I think it matters.

I am not a woman who buys things from Facebook. I am not a woman who falls for things. I worked the front desk at a pediatric practice for 24 years and I have heard every miracle pitch you can imagine from every essential-oil-pyramid-scheme cousin in the state of West Virginia. I am suspicious by trade.

So I read for 4 days before I took the first capsule.

Here's what I figured out, as a 58-year-old woman with no medical degree but a quarter century of sitting next to a doctor at lunch.

Your blood pressure is not a separate problem from the rest of your body. It is a downstream signal of what is happening on the inside of your blood vessels. The inside lining. The endothelium. When the lining is worn down, the lining produces less nitric oxide. Your vessels stay tight. Your heart has to push harder. The number on the cuff goes up.

Pills can lower the number. Pills cannot heal the lining.

body:
I sat on the mudroom floor of my own house last Tuesday night with my 14-year-old cat in my lap and my hands shaking so bad I couldn't work the latch on her carrier.

Pepper was wheezing. Not the regular asthma wheeze I've heard from her since 2019. The new wheeze. The bad one. The one I knew from 22 years of working at Dr. Halverson's clinic meant we were maybe 4 hours away from a real problem.

I had the carrier sitting open in front of me on the linoleum. Pink plastic, the one I'd bought her in 2011 when she was a kitten. I'd put a folded towel inside. I had my keys in my pocket. I had the after-hours number for the emergency clinic on Cedar Street pulled up on my phone.

And I could not get my fingers to close around that little plastic latch.

I tried with my right hand. My index finger and thumb wouldn't pinch hard enough. I tried with my left. Same. I tried with both hands at once and my wedding ring caught on the wire mesh and I started crying.

Pepper looked up at me with the look. If you've ever loved a cat that's older than your marriage, you know the look. She wasn't scared. She was patient. She was the one being patient with me.

That was the moment I knew something had to change.

I'd been telling myself for 18 months that my hands were "just acting up." That's what I'd say to my husband Dale when he asked. "Hands are just acting up today." Dale is a carpenter. He's been working with his hands since he was 16. He knows what hands are supposed to do. He'd stopped asking around January.

My name is Maureen. Most people call me Mo. I'm 56 years old. I live in a little ranch on the east side of Lansing, Michigan, two blocks from where I grew up. I worked as a veterinary technician at Halverson Animal Hospital for 22 years. Retired in October 2023 because my hands couldn't hold a syringe steady anymore. I told Dr. Halverson it was time. He cried. I cried. Then I went home and didn't get out of my pajamas for 11 days.

Pepper has been with me longer than my retirement, longer than my marriage to Dale, longer than my mother has been gone. I got her at the clinic in the spring of 2011. Somebody dropped her in a cardboard box on the back stoop with a note that said "her name is Pepper and we can't keep her, please be kind." She was 8 weeks old and she had one front tooth growing in sideways. I took her home that night and she's been mine ever since.

Dale was working in Saginaw on a kitchen remodel that Tuesday night. He'd left at 6 AM. He wouldn't be home until Wednesday afternoon.

So it was just me and Pepper on the mudroom floor.

I want to back up and explain how my hands got to be like that. Because if you've got hands that are starting to do this, you need to understand what was happening to mine. Because nobody explained it to me until much later. And by the time somebody did, I'd spent two years telling myself it was just one of those things.

It started slow. It always does. I'd be unscrewing a flea medication tube at work and my thumb would slip. I'd drop a leash. I'd fumble a pill into the wrong pile while I was counting out a script. Little stuff. Stuff I covered up by being faster everywhere else. I'd been doing the job for 22 years. My brain knew what my hands were supposed to do. My hands had just stopped listening as well.

Then it was bigger things. Opening a can of cat food. Buttoning the cuff of my work scrubs. Wringing out a sponge. By the summer of 2023 I was wearing pull-on pants exclusively because I couldn't manage a zipper without taking 3 tries.

I went to see Dr. Lawson, my primary, in August of 2023. He looked at my hands for maybe 90 seconds. He moved my fingers around. He pressed on the joints. He said "Maureen, this looks like wear and tear. You've spent 22 years restraining cats and dogs that didn't want to be restrained. You've put your hands through it. We can talk about a referral if you want, but honestly at your age this is what we see. Take some ibuprofen, ice them at night, and try not to overdo it."

I left his office and sat in my Honda Civic in the parking lot and stared at the steering wheel for 14 minutes.

Try not to overdo it.

I'd spent 22 years restraining a Mastiff that needed his anal glands expressed. I'd held a feral barn cat still for a spay while she tried to take my forearm off. I'd lifted a 94-pound Golden Retriever onto a surgical table by myself at 6:47 AM because the other tech called in sick.

Try not to overdo it.

I retired two months later. I didn't tell Dr. Lawson it was because of my hands. I told Dr. Halverson it was because of my hands and he told me the clinic would never replace me, which was kind, and he held my hands in both of his, gently, the way you hold something you know is broken, and he said "Mo, you go take care of yourself."

I didn't take care of myself. I sat on the couch.

For 14 months I sat on the couch and watched my hands get worse. I tried glucosamine. Two different brands. 7 months. Nothing. I tried turmeric capsules from the GNC at Frandor Mall. 4 months. Nothing. I tried a CBD cream a woman at church recommended that smelled like menthol and a barn. 3 weeks. Nothing.

I tried compression gloves I ordered off Amazon. I tried paraffin wax dips. I tried hot water soaks at the kitchen sink every morning before coffee. I tried the magnetic bracelet my sister sent me from Sedona.

Nothing.

By the time we get to last Tuesday night, when I was sitting on the mudroom floor with Pepper wheezing in my lap, my hands had been in that state for 18 months and I had given up on them.

I want to be honest about that. I had given up. I thought 56 was the new old. I thought this was what happened to women who'd worked with their hands. I thought I'd had a good run and now this was the cost.

I drove Pepper to the emergency clinic with the carrier door bungee-corded shut, because that's what I figured out at 9:47 PM on a Tuesday when my fingers wouldn't work. I bungee-corded the door of the carrier shut with an exercise band I keep in the mudroom. I sobbed all the way to Cedar Street.

Pepper turned out to be okay. They gave her a steroid shot and an oxygen treatment and sent us home at 11:24 PM with instructions to follow up with my regular vet within 48 hours.

My regular vet is Dr. Halverson. The man I'd worked for for 22 years.

I called the clinic Wednesday morning at 7:58 AM, two minutes before they opened, because I knew the receptionist Annette would be there starting the coffee. I told Annette what happened. She fit me in at 2:15 PM that afternoon.

I walked into Halverson Animal Hospital on Wednesday at 2:11 PM. Annette took Pepper from me at the front desk and gave me a hug. Then Dr. Halverson walked out from the back. He's 64 now. Grey beard, glasses, scrubs with little dachshunds on them that his wife gave him for Christmas in 2018.

He looked at my hands as I handed him Pepper's chart.

He didn't say anything right then. He took Pepper to the back, did her exam, came back 11 minutes later, said she was looking better, scheduled a follow-up in 10 days, and then he said, "Mo, can you come back to my office for a minute."

I followed him back. He shut the door.

He sat down across from me at his desk, which is the same desk I'd sat across from for 22 years discussing patient cases. The desk has a little brass nameplate that says Dr. R. Halverson, DVM. The desk has a framed photo of his three kids and his late wife Carolyn, who died in 2017. The desk has a wooden box of dog biscuits that he'd been refilling since 2003.

He said, "Mo. What's going on with your hands."

I told him. The whole thing. The mudroom floor. The bungee cord on the carrier. The 18 months. The glucosamine. The compression gloves. The CBD cream. Dr. Lawson telling me I'd just used my hands too much for too long.

He listened. He's good at that. He'd been good at it for 22 years.

When I was done, he leaned back in his chair and said this:

"Mo, when an old dog comes in here and his joints are shot, the first thing I think about isn't the joints. I think about why his cells stopped maintaining the joints. I want to back up and explain how my hands got to be like that. Because if you've got hands that are starting to do this, you need to understand what was happening to mine. Because nobody explained it to me until much later. And by the time somebody did, I'd spent two years telling myself it was just one of those things.

It started slow. It always does. I'd be unscrewing a flea medication tube at work and my thumb would slip. I'd drop a leash. I'd fumble a pill into the wrong pile while I was counting out a script. Little stuff. Stuff I covered up by being faster everywhere else. I'd been doing the job for 22 years. My brain knew what my hands were supposed to do. My hands had just stopped listening as well.

Then it was bigger things. Opening a can of cat food. Buttoning the cuff of my work scrubs. Wringing out a sponge. By the summer of 2023 I was wearing pull-on pants exclusively because I couldn't manage a zipper without taking 3 tries.

I went to see Dr. Lawson, my primary, in August of 2023. He looked at my hands for maybe 90 seconds. He moved my fingers around. He pressed on the joints. He said "Maureen, this looks like wear and tear. You've spent 22 years restraining cats and dogs that didn't want to be restrained. You've put your hands through it. We can talk about a referral if you want, but honestly at your age this is what we see. Take some ibuprofen, ice them at night, and try not to overdo it."

I left his office and sat in my Honda Civic in the parking lot and stared at the steering wheel for 14 minutes.

Try not to overdo it.

I'd spent 22 years restraining a Mastiff that needed his anal glands expressed. I'd held a feral barn cat still for a spay while she tried to take my forearm off. I'd lifted a 94-pound Golden Retriever onto a surgical table by myself at 6:47 AM because the other tech called in sick.

Try not to overdo it.

I retired two months later. I didn't tell Dr. Lawson it was because of my hands. I told Dr. Halverson it was because of my hands and he told me the clinic would never replace me, which was kind, and he held my hands in both of his, gently, the way you hold something you know is broken, and he said "Mo, you go take care of yourself."

I didn't take care of myself. I sat on the couch.

For 14 months I sat on the couch and watched my hands get worse. I tried glucosamine. Two different brands. 7 months. Nothing. I tried turmeric capsules from the GNC at Frandor Mall. 4 months. Nothing. I tried a CBD cream a woman at church recommended that smelled like menthol and a barn. 3 weeks. Nothing.

I tried compression gloves I ordered off Amazon. I tried paraffin wax dips. I tried hot water soaks at the kitchen sink every morning before coffee. I tried the magnetic bracelet my sister sent me from Sedona.

Nothing.

By the time we get to last Tuesday night, when I was sitting on the mudroom floor with Pepper wheezing in my lap, my hands had been in that state for 18 months and I had given up on them.

I want to be honest about that. I had given up. I thought 56 was the new old. I thought this was what happened to women who'd worked with their hands. I thought I'd had a good run and now this was the cost.

I drove Pepper to the emergency clinic with the carrier door bungee-corded shut, because that's what I figured out at 9:47 PM on a Tuesday when my fingers wouldn't work. I bungee-corded the door of the carrier shut with an exercise band I keep in the mudroom. I sobbed all the way to Cedar Street.

Pepper turned out to be okay. They gave her a steroid shot and an oxygen treatment and sent us home at 11:24 PM with instructions to follow up with my regular vet within 48 hours.

My regular vet is Dr. Halverson. The man I'd worked for for 22 years.

I called the clinic Wednesday morning at 7:58 AM, two minutes before they opened, because I knew the receptionist Annette would be there starting the coffee. I told Annette what happened. She fit me in at 2:15 PM that afternoon.

I walked into Halverson Animal Hospital on Wednesday at 2:11 PM. Annette took Pepper from me at the front desk and gave me a hug. Then Dr. Halverson walked out from the back. He's 64 now. Grey beard, glasses, scrubs with little dachshunds on them that his wife gave him for Christmas in 2018.

He looked at my hands as I handed him Pepper's chart.

He didn't say anything right then. He took Pepper to the back, did her exam, came back 11 minutes later, said she was looking better, scheduled a follow-up in 10 days, and then he said, "Mo, can you come back to my office for a minute."

I followed him back. He shut the door.

He sat down across from me at his desk, which is the same desk I'd sat across from for 22 years discussing patient cases. The desk has a little brass nameplate that says Dr. R. Halverson, DVM. The desk has a framed photo of his three kids and his late wife Carolyn, who died in 2017. The desk has a wooden box of dog biscuits that he'd been refilling since 2003.

He said, "Mo. What's going on with your hands."

I told him. The whole thing. The mudroom floor. The bungee cord on the carrier. The 18 months. The glucosamine. The compression gloves. The CBD cream. Dr. Lawson telling me I'd just used my hands too much for too long.

He listened. He's good at that. He'd been good at it for 22 years.

When I was done, he leaned back in his chair and said this:

"Mo, when an old dog comes in here and his joints are shot, the first thing I think about isn't the joints. I think about why his cells stopped maintaining the joints. Because joints don't just give up. Joints are kept healthy by the cells inside them. And those cells need fuel to do their job. When the cells stop getting fuel, the joints stop being maintained. The cartilage starts going. The lubrication thins out. The whole machine grinds."

He pointed at his own knee.

"That's what we treat in geriatric dogs. We don't just treat the knee. We treat the cells that are supposed to be taking care of the knee."

He paused.

"My wife had what you have, Mo. Carolyn. Her hands toward the end. We'd been to three specialists. Nobody helped."

I knew about Carolyn's hands. I'd watched her decline for two years before she died. It wasn't her hands that killed her. But her hands had been the first thing to go.

He said, "I've been reading. The last 14 months. I started reading because my own hands started doing this. Look."

He held up his right hand. There was a slight tremor I hadn't noticed.

"I'm 64 and I work surgery 4 days a week. I cannot have hands that don't work. So I went looking. And what I found is that the cells in your joints, the ones that are supposed to be maintaining cartilage and managing inflammation and keeping things lubricated, they need a kind of cellular energy. That energy gets made inside every cell by these tiny structures called mitochondria. They're your body's power plants."

I knew what mitochondria were. Anyone who's worked in a vet clinic for 22 years has heard mitochondria mentioned more than once. We see mitochondrial issues in geriatric pets. We see it in cats with kidney disease. We see it constantly.

"When the mitochondria are healthy and humming, your joint cells get the energy they need to do their job. When the mitochondria get worn down, by years of stress and processed food and toxin exposure and just being alive in 2026, your joint cells start running on empty. The cells stop maintaining the joints. The joints stop working."

He leaned forward.

"Everything you tried, Mo, the glucosamine, the turmeric, all of it, that stuff is trying to deliver materials to a building site that doesn't have any workers. The workers are gone. The cells aren't doing their job because they don't have the energy. You can dump a truckload of glucosamine on the site and nothing gets built. The cells have to be able to do the work."

He pulled a small green bottle out of his desk drawer.

"This is what I've been taking for 8 months."

The label said Auniva. The capsules inside were a deep green-brown color.

"It's amla. It's a fruit. Indian gooseberry. The Ayurvedic medicine people have been using it for thousands of years for what they used to call 'aging.' What it appears to do, mechanism-wise, is support a pathway in your body called AMPK. Think of AMPK as the foreman that tells your mitochondria to get back to work. When AMPK is active, your mitochondria can start producing cellular energy more efficiently, the way they did when you were younger."

He set the bottle on the desk between us.

"When the mitochondria are humming again, the cells in your joints can get back to doing their job. Maintaining the cartilage. Managing the inflammation. Lubricating. The materials you've already got in your body can finally get used."

He flexed his right hand.

"My tremor's gone. I did surgery on a Great Dane on Monday that lasted 3 hours and 14 minutes. I'd have had to hand that off to a colleague a year ago."

I sat there looking at the bottle.

He said, "It's not a miracle. It's a tool. But it's the only thing I've found that actually addresses why this is happening to women your age and men my age. Everything else treats the symptom."

I asked him where to get it.

He wrote it down on the back of Pepper's discharge paperwork. auniva.co/amla/33. He said the company has a 90-day money-back guarantee, which is what got him to try it in the first place. He said, "Mo, if it doesn't work for you, you send it back and they give you your money. That's a fair deal. That's better than I got from any of the supplements I tried for Carolyn."

I ordered it from my car in the parking lot before I drove home. I sat there at 3:14 PM with Pepper in her bungee-corded carrier in the passenger seat and I pulled out my phone and I ordered a bottle.

I want to slow down for a second and talk about that bottle. Because I'd ordered enough useless bottles over the previous 18 months that I'd lost count.

I want to be specific about what's different about this one.

The first thing is the mechanism. When I'd taken glucosamine, I'd never been able to find a clear explanation of what the glucosamine was actually doing once it got into my body. I asked Dr. Lawson once. He shrugged. He said it might help. Maybe.

Amla is different. The mechanism is specific. AMPK activation. Mitochondrial support. Antioxidant protection of those mitochondria from oxidative stress. The same mechanism Dr. Halverson talked about for old dogs. The same mechanism I'd learned about in textbooks 25 years ago in vet tech school.

The second thing is the antioxidant profile. Amla has one of the highest antioxidant concentrations of any food ever measured. Higher than blueberries by a wide margin. The antioxidants are part of why the mechanism holds together. The same oxidative stress that wears your mitochondria down in the first place is what amla helps protect against. So it's not just getting the foreman back. It's protecting the power plants from the thing that wore them down to begin with.

The third thing is the guarantee. 90 days. Not 30. 30 days isn't long enough to know whether something is working for hands that have been failing for 18 months. 90 days is enough to actually see. And if you don't see it, you send the bottle back and they refund you. Every penny. Dr. Halverson told me he'd never actually tested the guarantee because his hands worked again by week 5. But it was there.

The bottle came on a Friday. I took the first two capsules with my breakfast Saturday morning, March 22nd.

Week one I didn't feel anything. I want to be honest about that, because there are people who write these things and pretend the first dose was a thunderbolt. It wasn't. Week one I took the capsules and felt nothing and almost emailed the company on day 6 to ask if I'd gotten a placebo by mistake.

Day 11 I unscrewed the lid on a jar of strawberry preserves Dale's mother had sent over. I didn't notice I'd done it until I was already spreading them on toast.

Day 14 I opened a can of cat food with the pull tab. I'd been using the electric can opener for 9 months.

Day 19 I picked up Pepper, all 11 pounds of her, with both arms instead of scooping her with my forearms.

Day 23 I buttoned the cuff of a flannel shirt without looking.

Day 27 Dale came home from a job site, watched me sign a check at the kitchen counter, and said, "Mo, your handwriting."

My handwriting had been sloppy for 2 years. He'd watched me struggle to sign a Christmas card the previous December and not said anything. Now he was standing in the kitchen with his work boots still on staring at a check I'd just signed and his eyes were wet.

Day 34 I drove down to Halverson's for Pepper's follow-up. I carried her in the pink carrier, no bungee cord, latched it myself, held it in one hand. Dr. Halverson watched me do it from across the waiting room.

He didn't say anything. He just smiled.

I have been on Auniva Amla for 7 weeks now. My hands aren't 26 again. I want to be clear about that. They're 56. But they're 56 hands that work. 56 hands that close. 56 hands that grip. 56 hands that buttoned the back of a sundress on Mother's Day for the first time in 4 years.

Dale knows. He won't say it directly, because he's a man who builds things and men who build things don't talk about feelings out loud. But last Sunday he came home with a hand-thrown ceramic mug from a craft fair in Old Town and he set it in front of me at breakfast and said, "I got you a new mug. I thought you might want something nice to hold."

I cried into my coffee for 11 minutes.

If you're reading this, and you've got hands that are starting to do what mine were doing, I want you to hear me.

You don't have 18 more months to give to this. Nobody does. The years where your hands work are not unlimited. They are not a resource you get back. Every month you spend on the wrong supplement is a month you don't get a do-over on.

Auniva has a 90-day money-back guarantee. Take it for 90 days. Three bottles. If your hands are not closing the way they used to, you send the bottles back and they refund you. No phone call. No fine print. The glucosamine I took for 7 months didn't come with a guarantee. The compression gloves didn't. The magnetic bracelet didn't. The 14 months I sat on my couch waiting for my hands to get better didn't come with a refund either.

This does.

P.S. You'll know it's working before you can prove it. For Dr. Halverson it was a Great Dane surgery. For me it was a jar of strawberry preserves. It won't be a thunderbolt. It'll be a moment where you do something you'd given up on doing, and you'll do it without thinking, and then 30 seconds later you'll realize what just happened, and you'll have to sit down. Mark the date when it happens. You'll want to remember.

P.P.S. About that 90-day guarantee. Most companies give you 30. Most. 30 days is not enough time for a body that has been running on tired mitochondria for a decade. Auniva gives you 90, which is the actual amount of time it takes to know. The only reason a company offers a guarantee that long is because they know what's going to happen inside those 90 days. They've watched it happen. They're confident.

P.P.P.S. Dr. Halverson told me Auniva is a small company and they sometimes sell out. He had to wait 9 days for his third bottle in January and started rationing the second one so he wouldn't run out. I keep two bottles in the kitchen drawer now where Dale keeps his measuring tape. One open, one sealed. Pepper is 14 years old and the vet who used to be my boss told me she might have 2 more good years in her. I am not going back to bungee-cording her carrier shut. Not for one day.

P.P.P.P.S. If you have a mother, a sister, a wife, a daughter, an aunt, anyone whose hands have been slowly failing her and who keeps saying "they're just acting up today," send this to her. Send it without a message. Just the link. She'll know what to do.

The pink carrier is back in the closet. The bungee cord is back in the drawer. Pepper is on the couch next to me right now, asleep on a flannel blanket, the same blanket I folded one-handed last night before I came to bed.

These are hands that work again.

body:
I forgot a woman's name at the Publix on Forest Drive and sat in my car for 10 minutes afterward.

It was a Wednesday morning, around 10:30, and I was in the produce section pinching avocados the way my mother taught me to. I had my list in my pocket. I had nowhere to be. I was the most relaxed I'd been all week, and that's the part that's important, because what happened next happened to a relaxed woman in good spirits, which is not the version of me you'd expect to fall apart.

A voice said, "Patricia."

I turned around.

The woman was in her mid 40s. Blonde hair pulled back. Cream colored cardigan. A toddler in the cart who had to be a grandchild, because she was too put together for a young mother and her face had that 40-something softness.

She said my name like we were friends.

She smiled at me the way you smile at somebody you've shared something with. She said, "Oh my goodness, it's been so long. How are you?" And she came around the avocado bin with her arms half open, the way somebody does when they're going in for the hug but they're checking to see if you want one too.

And I stood there with an avocado in my hand and I had absolutely no idea who she was.

I knew I knew her. I knew it deep in some part of me that wasn't connecting to whatever part is supposed to know names. Her face was familiar in a way that made it worse. If she'd been a total stranger I could have just said, "I'm sorry, I think you have me confused with someone else." But I knew her. We had history. And the history was just gone.

I did what you do.

I hugged her. I said, "Oh my goodness, it's been forever. How are you?" I asked about her, generally, in the kind of vague way you can ask without giving anything away. She told me her oldest had gotten into Clemson. I made the appropriate sounds. She told me she'd retired from the district 2 years ago. I felt something cold move down my back, because if she'd been with the district, I had almost certainly known her name as well as I knew the names of my own children.

She talked for about 4 minutes. I nodded. I smiled. I asked about her husband, generically. She told me about her husband, whose name I also did not retrieve. She told me about a vacation they were taking. She said she'd been meaning to call me. She said we should get coffee.

And then she said, "Well, I'll let you finish your shopping. So good to see you, Patricia."

She hugged me again. She wheeled her cart away. The toddler waved at me over her shoulder.

I stood there with the avocado in my hand.

I put it in my cart. I picked up a different one. I put that one in my cart too. I walked over to the bananas. I stood by the bananas for what felt like 2 minutes. My heart was going. My hands had that buzzing feeling you get when you've had too much coffee.

I left my cart there.

I walked out of the Publix without buying a single thing. I got in my car. I put my hands on the steering wheel. I sat there in the parking lot with my hands on the wheel and the air conditioning off and the August sun coming through the windshield, and I tried to remember her name.

It didn't come.

I sat there for 10 minutes.

It still didn't come.

I drove home, and I made it almost to my driveway, and I had to pull over on Heyward Street because I was crying.

Her name was Linda Coker.

I remembered it 3 days later, on a Saturday morning, while I was watering the ferns on the front porch. Just like that. The name fell into my head out of the air. Linda Coker, the head of the special education department at Carver Elementary, who I had worked with for 11 years, who had organized my retirement luncheon in 2019, who had given me a framed photograph of all the teachers signed on the matte that's hanging in my office right now.

Linda Coker.

I sat down on the porch step with the watering can in my hand and I cried again, but this time for a different reason. Relief, partly. Shame, mostly.

Because Linda's name should not have taken 3 days.

I'm Patricia Whitman. I'm 63 years old. I was the principal at Carver Elementary School in Columbia, South Carolina, for 17 years before I retired in 2019. I have a master's degree from the University of South Carolina. I have served on the boards of 2 different community education non-profits. I gave a 25 minute keynote address at a state principals' conference in 2014 without any notes. My memory has been a piece of professional equipment for my entire adult life, and the equipment is starting to fail.

I want to tell you something I have not told my husband or my sister or my best friend Marjorie, which is that the Publix wasn't the first time. It was the time I couldn't deny anymore. But it wasn't the first.

A month before the Publix, I'd been at a doctor's appointment and the front desk woman asked me my date of birth and there was a half second where I could not retrieve it. Half a second. Long enough to feel it but not long enough that the woman noticed. I told her my birthday and she typed it in and the appointment went on.

Two weeks before the Publix, I'd been telling my husband Ed a story about something that had happened at the bank, and I forgot the word for the form they make you sign. Just the regular form. I sat there in my own kitchen looking at my own husband and said, "And so I had to sign the, the, you know, the thing with the lines." The word "deposit slip" came back to me about a minute later. Ed didn't say anything. He didn't make a thing of it. He just nodded along like nothing had happened.

It's the little things that scare you the most. The big things you can pretend are flukes. The little things tell you the truth.

I made myself a list one night about a week after the Publix.

I sat at my desk in the room that used to be my home office and I wrote down every time in the previous 6 months I could remember something not coming when it was supposed to. I wrote down 23 incidents. 23 in 6 months. The day I forgot the gas station was on the right instead of the left. The afternoon I called my niece Susan by my sister's name. The morning I couldn't think of the word for the spice that goes in pumpkin pie until I'd been standing in front of the spice rack for 4 minutes. Nutmeg. Of course nutmeg.

23 incidents that I could remember.

I sat at my desk with my list and I thought, "Patricia, this is the thing you don't want to think about."

My mother had developed dementia in her 70s. I had watched it happen. I had been in the assisted living facility the day she'd called me Margaret, which was her sister's name, who had been dead for 22 years at that point. I had held her hand and said, "Mom. I'm Patricia. I'm your daughter." And she had looked at me with those wide bright eyes and said, "Of course, sweetheart," in the way she said it when she was just going along with what I was telling her without knowing it.

I'd told myself I was going to do everything I could not to be her at the end.

And here I was, 63 years old, with 23 incidents on a piece of paper in front of me.

I called my doctor's office the next morning. I told the woman on the phone that I wanted to talk to Dr. Mehta about memory concerns. She put me down for 3 weeks out.

The 3 weeks felt like 3 years.

In those 3 weeks I read.

I want to tell you what I read because the reading is what changed my life. I want to be clear about something first. I am not telling you reading saved me from dementia. I am not telling you anything will or won't save you from dementia. I am not a doctor and I do not know what your future or my future holds. What I am telling you is what I learned about my brain in those 3 weeks, that nobody had ever sat me down and explained, and what I started doing about it.

The first thing I learned was that the brain is the single most energy hungry organ in the body. By a wide margin. Your brain is about 2 percent of your body weight and it uses about 20 percent of your daily energy. It is a furnace.

And the energy that powers that furnace is produced by little structures inside every brain cell called mitochondria.

I had not thought about mitochondria since 11th grade biology. I went and read about them like I was studying for a test. Mitochondria produce the energy that runs every cell in your body, but they're especially critical to brain cells. Your neurons fire constantly. They are working all day, every day. They need a constant, reliable, clean supply of energy. And the structures that produce that energy take damage over time. The byproducts of normal energy production create a kind of oxidative stress, and that stress accumulates inside the mitochondria year after year. Researchers have a name for the result. They call it mitochondrial dysfunction.

And one of the most studied areas in neuroscience right now is the connection between mitochondrial dysfunction and exactly the kind of slow, frustrating, scary cognitive changes I had been writing on my list.

The forgotten names. The lost words. The half second pauses.

It's not always dementia. Sometimes it is, and sometimes it isn't. But the underlying mechanism, the mitochondrial side of it, is something researchers are taking very seriously, and the reason is that when you understand the mechanism you start to see the openings. You start to see the places where the body might be supported in doing what it's been doing all along. You start to see that "this is just aging" is not the only story available.

I read deeper. I read for hours every night that month. Ed would come in and ask if I was coming to bed and I'd say give me 20 more minutes, and 90 minutes later I'd still be at the desk with the lamp on.

The thing that kept coming up was a compound called urolithin A.

Urolithin A is something your body produces when your gut bacteria break down certain dietary polyphenols. The richest source of the precursors that get converted into urolithin A is pomegranate. Specifically the concentrated polyphenols in the peel and the rind.

And the reason urolithin A has gotten so much research attention recently, including a 2024 study out of the University of Copenhagen that I want to be careful with because the research is still developing and a lot of it is still preclinical, is that urolithin A appears to support a process called mitophagy. Mitophagy is the body's own housekeeping system for clearing out damaged mitochondria so that newer, healthier ones can take their place. It's a process the body has been running for as long as you've been alive. And when it's running well, the cells, including the brain cells, have access to cleaner energy.

When researchers have looked at urolithin A specifically in the context of brain mitochondria, the early signals have been interesting enough that they're now planning clinical trials in humans with cognitive issues.

I want to say it again. I am not telling you this is a cure for anything. I am not a doctor. The research is still developing. What I'm telling you is that there is a mechanism being studied that addresses a real biological process that I, at 63 years old, have likely been losing ground on for the last 20 years.

I read about pomegranate research in other areas too. There have been studies on pomegranate extract and memory. A small double-blind study of middle aged and older adults showed improved verbal and visual memory after 4 weeks of pomegranate juice. A trial at UCLA in adults aged 50 to 75 looking at pomegranate extract found positive signals in cognitive performance at multiple checkpoints. A 2024 trial in 80 individuals dealing with mild cognitive concerns found significantly better outcomes with pomegranate seed oil supplementation alongside a Mediterranean diet compared to diet alone, across global cognition, verbal episodic memory, and processing and executive functions.

I sat at my desk and I read all of this and I thought about Linda Coker.

I thought about my mother.

I thought about the form at the bank.

I thought about 23 incidents in 6 months on a piece of paper.

And I ordered a bottle of Auniva.

Auniva Pomegranate. 2 capsules a day. Made in the US. The concentrated extract from the peel where the active compounds are most highly concentrated. 30 servings per bottle. A 90 day money back guarantee, which I noticed and which mattered to me because at 63 years old I am tired of giving companies my money for products they don't stand behind.

I went to the doctor 9 days after I ordered the bottle. I had the bottle in my purse.

Dr. Mehta is a thoughtful woman. She listened to me for almost 25 minutes. I told her about the Publix. I told her about the list. I told her about my mother. She gave me a cognitive screening test in the office that day, the kind they give you to establish a baseline. She said my results were normal for my age and education. She told me to come back in 6 months and we'd do it again.

She did not dismiss me. I want to be clear about that. She took me seriously. She just also told me that what I was describing was within the range of normal age related cognitive change, and that there was nothing she could prescribe at this point.

I asked her what she thought about pomegranate extract.

She paused. She said, "Patricia, there's some interesting early research. It's not at the level where I would prescribe it. But as a supplement, I don't have any concerns about it. Make sure your supplements and your medications don't conflict and let me know what you're taking."

I told her about the Auniva.

She wrote it in my chart.

I started taking it the next morning.

I want to tell you about the last 4 months because the last 4 months are why I'm writing this.

The first 3 weeks I didn't notice much. I want to say that honestly. I think I was looking too hard. I'd find myself, in the middle of a sentence, asking myself "did that come faster than it would have a month ago." And the answer was usually I don't know. The brain is bad at noticing what it's doing.

Around week 5, something else started happening that I want to tell you about because it surprised me.

I was sleeping better.

I hadn't realized I was sleeping badly until I was sleeping better. Ed and I had been having those middle of the night moments where one of us would be awake at 3 AM and the other would notice and we'd both end up reading on our phones for an hour. They had become so normal we'd stopped commenting on them. Around week 5 I noticed I'd slept through, 4 nights in a row.

By week 7, I noticed I was reading more.

I had been a 4 books a year reader for the last 3 years, which was a disgrace for a person who had run a school for 17 years. I would pick up a book and read 6 pages and lose interest. I started a book in late September and finished it 9 days later. Then I started another one. By the end of November I'd finished 4 books, which used to be my pace in college.

By week 10, I was teaching a Sunday school class for adults.

I want to be careful, again. I don't know what's causing what. I'm not telling you the pomegranate is doing all of it. I pointed to the wrong child at my granddaughter's piano recital last March and I drove home in silence afterward and I sat in my own driveway for 22 minutes before I could make myself go inside the house.

That is where this story starts. Not in a hospital. Not in a doctor's office. In a Honda Civic in a driveway on James Island, South Carolina, with the engine off and my hands on the steering wheel and the late afternoon light coming through the windshield, trying to convince myself that what had just happened in that recital hall was not what I knew it was.

My name is Marlene. I'm 59 years old. I am a retired second grade teacher. I taught at the same elementary school in West Ashley for 28 years. I retired in 2021 because my husband Glenn had a heart scare and I wanted to be home more.

Glenn is fine now. Glenn is 63 and Glenn putters around the yard and Glenn drives me crazy in the kitchen and Glenn is exactly the man he has always been.

I am the one who is not exactly the woman I have always been.

I have one daughter, Ashley. Ashley is 34. Ashley lives 8 minutes from us in a little cottage off Folly Road with her husband Brett and their two kids. The oldest is my granddaughter Cora. Cora is 7. Cora has been taking piano lessons since she was 5 from a woman named Mrs. Pelletier who teaches out of her sun room in Riverland Terrace.

The recital was on a Sunday afternoon in March. 3 PM. At a Lutheran church on Camp Road that Mrs. Pelletier rents twice a year for these things. Glenn was out of town. He was in Greenville at his brother's lake house for the weekend doing some kind of fishing thing he does every year. So it was me, alone, in a pew, with a program in my hand and a bouquet of pink carnations on the seat next to me that I'd picked up from the Harris Teeter on the way over.

Cora was scheduled to play 9th, in the second half. She had been practicing "Annie's Song" by John Denver. She had been practicing it since January. I had heard it on Sunday afternoons at Ashley's house roughly 800 times.

The recital started. Children played. Parents clapped. There were 14 students that year, ranging from 5 years old to 12. They sat in the front three rows in little dresses and clip-on ties and patent leather shoes, waiting their turn.

The boy next to Cora was a kid named Eli, who was 8. He had blonde hair and a navy bow tie and he was kicking the back of the pew in front of him the entire first half of the recital and his mother kept reaching forward and putting a hand on his knee to make him stop.

I knew all of this. I had been watching all of it for 40 minutes.

We hit intermission. Mrs. Pelletier announced a 10 minute break. People got up to use the restroom and stretch their legs.

A woman I had never seen before came up the aisle and stopped at my pew. She was around my age. She was wearing a green blouse and reading glasses on a chain.

She smiled at me and she said, "Excuse me, I'm sorry to bother you, but I am here to see my niece play and I'm a little turned around. Which one of these little ones is yours?"

She was being friendly. She was making small talk. It was a totally ordinary moment in a totally ordinary church on a totally ordinary Sunday afternoon.

I lifted my hand and I pointed.

I pointed at a little girl in the third row in a yellow dress with brown hair in two French braids.

The woman said, "Oh, isn't she sweet."

She walked away.

I sat there with my finger half raised.

The little girl in the yellow dress with the brown hair in two French braids was not Cora.

Cora was in the front row.

Cora was in a navy blue dress with white piping. Her hair was down with a little pink ribbon in it. She was sitting right next to the kicking boy Eli.

The little girl in the yellow dress was a child I had never seen before in my life.

I had pointed at a stranger.

I had pointed at a stranger and identified her as my own granddaughter.

I had been watching Cora the entire first half. I had been watching Eli kick the pew next to her. I had been watching her play with the bow on her dress when she got nervous. And the second somebody asked me a simple question, my brain had reached into a drawer that was supposed to have Cora in it, and it had pulled out a stranger.

For 30 seconds.

For 30 seconds, I had pointed at the wrong child and called her mine.

I sat in that pew and I felt something cold move through my body that I have never felt before or since.

It was not embarrassment. The woman was gone. The woman did not know.

It was something deeper than embarrassment.

It was the feeling of finding out, in a single small moment, that the inside of you has been quietly slipping for longer than you have wanted to admit.

I made it through the rest of the recital. Cora played "Annie's Song" beautifully and made one tiny mistake at the bridge and recovered like a professional and I clapped and I cried a little, the way grandmas are supposed to cry, and I gave her the carnations and I hugged her and I told her I was so proud of her.

Ashley said, "Mama, you want to come back to the house? We're doing pizza."

I told her I had a headache. I told her I'd see them on Wednesday. I drove home.

I sat in my driveway for 22 minutes.

The thing is.

It wasn't the first time.

I had been pretending it was the first time. I had been pretending all the little moments before it didn't count. I had been pretending that the day I called Glenn by my father's name (my father has been dead since 2003) was a joke. That the time at the Publix when I couldn't remember the word "sponge" and stood in the cleaning aisle for 6 minutes trying to think of it was just because I was distracted. That the day I left my phone in the refrigerator next to the eggs was just because I was tired.

I had been pretending.

The recital broke the pretending.

I sat in that driveway and I let myself say the thing I had been refusing to say.

Something was happening to my brain.

Not in a dramatic way. Not in a hospital way. In a slow, quiet, terrifying way that I had been managing with humor and excuses for at least 2 years.

I knew what people my age were supposed to worry about. Everybody knows. We all have a friend whose mother went down that road. We all have an aunt who didn't recognize her own kids by the end. We all have a story we don't tell at parties.

I had been telling myself I was too young.

I am 59.

I am not too young for things to start shifting. I just had not been ready to admit they had started.

I sat in that driveway and I made myself a promise.

I was going to figure out what was happening to me.

Not because I was sure it was the worst thing. I was not sure. I am still not sure. I was going to figure out what was happening because the alternative, the pretending, the laughing it off, the calling Glenn by my father's name and shrugging, that was not a life I wanted to keep living.

I wanted to know what was actually going on.

I went inside the house. I made myself a cup of tea. I sat at the kitchen table.

I went to my doctor on Tuesday. I am going to tell you what happened at that appointment because I think a lot of women my age need to hear it.

I told her everything. The recital. The Publix sponge moment. Calling Glenn by my father's name. The phone in the refrigerator. The way I had been losing words mid sentence. The way I had been walking into rooms and forgetting why.

She listened. She was kind. She was 38 years old and she was kind.

She had me do a little test in the office. She asked me to count backwards from 100 by 7s. She asked me to remember three words. She asked me to draw a clock and put the hands at 10 past 11.

I did fine.

She told me I did fine.

She told me that what I was describing sounded like normal aging. She told me that everybody loses words sometimes. She told me that everybody puts the phone in weird places sometimes. She told me that pointing at the wrong child was likely just a brain hiccup, the kind anybody has when they get caught off guard.

She said, "Marlene, you're not in any cognitive danger zone right now. Your memory is going to be a little less sharp than it was at 35. That's normal."

I left her office with the same nothing I had walked in with.

She had been kind. She had been thorough. She had not lied to me.

But she had also not told me what was happening underneath the surface of my brain. She had told me I was fine. She had not told me why I, a woman who had memorized the names of 28 years of second graders, could not pull up the name of her own granddaughter when a stranger asked her at a piano recital.

I went home that Tuesday. I sat at the kitchen table again.

And for the first time in my life I did something I had spent my whole career as a teacher rolling my eyes at parents for doing.

I went on the internet to figure out what was wrong with me.

I sat at that kitchen table for 4 nights in a row after Glenn went to bed. I read until 1 AM. I read until 2 AM. I read with a notebook next to me and a pencil and I took notes the way I used to take notes when I was studying for my teaching certification in 1988.

I want to tell you what I found, because I think it matters.

I found out that inside every cell in your body, there are little structures called mitochondria. They are tiny. They are the part of your cells that produce energy. They are sometimes called the powerhouses of the cell.

I remembered that phrase from 7th grade science class. Powerhouses of the cell. I had taught that phrase to second graders in a unit on the human body. I had not thought about mitochondria once since 1992.

But the mitochondria are not just in the cells in your arms and legs. They are in the cells in your brain. They are in the neurons that fire when you remember a name. They are in the connections that pull a face out of a drawer when somebody asks you a question.

Your brain runs on mitochondria.

When you are young, your brain has plenty of healthy mitochondria. Your neurons fire clean and fast. You remember names. You pull words out without thinking. You watch a granddaughter for 40 minutes and you can point to her in a second.

But over the years, the mitochondria get worn down.

I sat at my kitchen table and I read this for the first time at 1 AM on a Wednesday in March and I cried a little.

Not from fear.

From recognition.

The mitochondria get worn down by stress. By poor sleep. By processed food. By environmental toxins. By aging itself. By 28 years of teaching second graders, which is a thing I am throwing in there for myself but which I believe to be biologically true.

Damaged mitochondria do not produce energy as cleanly. They start producing what the researchers called oxidative stress as a side product. Like a car with a worn out engine that starts coughing exhaust into its own cabin.

And the brain, of all the organs in your body, is the most demanding of clean mitochondrial energy. The brain uses about 20% of all the energy your body makes, even though it is only 2% of your body weight. When the mitochondria in your brain cells start sputtering, the brain feels it first.

Not in a dramatic way.

In a way that looks like pointing at the wrong child for 30 seconds.

In a way that looks like the word "sponge" not coming when you call it.

In a way that looks like calling your husband by your father's name.

I sat at that table and I felt every small moment of the last 2 years click into place.

This was not just aging. This was not just being 59. This was a specific thing happening inside the cells of my brain. A thing that had a name. A thing that researchers had been studying for decades. A thing that nobody, including the kind 38 year old doctor in her office on a Tuesday, had ever mentioned to me.

The next night I went back to the kitchen table and I kept reading.

I read about something called mitophagy. It is the word for the process the body uses to clean out damaged mitochondria and replace them with healthy ones. It is a thing your body does naturally. It is one of the body's most basic housekeeping functions.

But mitophagy slows down as you age. The damaged mitochondria stop getting cleared the way they used to. They pile up. They keep coughing exhaust into the cells. And the cells, especially the brain cells, suffer for it.

And then I read about a compound called urolithin A.

I had never heard of it.

Urolithin A, the article said, is a compound that researchers have been studying for its role in stimulating mitophagy. In helping the body do its housekeeping. In helping it clear out the damaged mitochondria and let the healthy ones do their job.

I read this very carefully. I read it twice. I am a retired teacher and I am not going to pretend I understood every word the first time.

The article said that urolithin A is produced in your gut, when your gut bacteria break down certain compounds you eat. The most studied source of those compounds, by a wide margin, is pomegranate.

Pomegranate.

The fruit my grandmother Coralee used to buy at the farmer's market in McClellanville every fall and eat at her kitchen table.

The article said that pomegranate contains compounds called punicalagins. Some of the most studied antioxidant compounds in all of nature. The article said pomegranate has one of the highest antioxidant profiles ever measured in a food. The article said ancient healers had called it the fruit of life for thousands of years and that there was a reason that name had stuck.

The punicalagins, when they get to your gut, are converted into urolithin A. The urolithin A then circulates through the body. And the research suggests it can help support the cellular housekeeping process that has been slowing down as you have been aging.

The damaged mitochondria can get cleared.

The cells, especially the brain cells, can run cleaner.

The body can do what it always knew how to do.

I sat at my kitchen table at 2:14 in the morning on a Thursday in March and I underlined that paragraph three times in my notebook.

I want to be very careful about how I describe what I felt next.

I did not feel like I had found a miracle. I am 59 years old and I have not believed in miracles since I was a child.

I felt like I had found a reasonable explanation for what was happening inside my body, and a reasonable thing to try that was not a prescription drug, that was not an injection, that was not a procedure, and that had research behind it going back decades.

That was all I had been looking for.

A reasonable explanation. A reasonable thing to try.

I kept reading. I read about a brand called Auniva.

I want to tell you why I chose them, because I am a careful woman with my money and I do not buy things on the internet without a reason.

Auniva did not promise me anything. They did not tell me their pomegranate was going to make me 30 again. They did not have a doctor in a white coat pointing at a brain scan. They explained the science. They explained the punicalagins. They explained what the research suggested and what it did not. They were honest about it in a way I had not seen on any of the other websites I had looked at.

And they backed every bottle with a 90 day money back guarantee. Which meant if it did not work for me, I could ship the bottle back inside 90 days and they would refund every penny.

That last part mattered. That meant I was not gambling. I was testing.

I ordered one bottle that Friday morning.

It came on a Wednesday.

I started that Thursday morning. One capsule with a glass of water before breakfast. I did not tell Glenn. I did not tell Ashley. I did not tell anybody. I wanted to see what happened without anybody watching me for it.

I want to tell you what happened over the next 12 weeks, and I want you to know I am not exaggerating any of it.

Week 1, nothing. I expected nothing. The article had said the process is slow because the cellular housekeeping takes time.

Week 2, nothing I could put my finger on. I was waiting for something dramatic. I did not get it.

Week 3, I noticed something small. I was reading a novel one night before bed and I realized I had read 40 pages and I could remember every plot point. I had been struggling to remember what I had read by morning for at least a year. I had been blaming the books. I had been telling myself I was picking boring ones.

It had not been the books.

Week 5, I was at the Publix and I was in the cleaning aisle. I caught myself.

I was in the cleaning aisle and I had walked there on purpose to buy sponges. I had remembered the word. I had remembered it without searching for it. I had walked in, gone to the aisle, picked up the sponges, and put them in my cart.

I stood there with the sponges in my hand for a minute and I just laughed, quietly, by myself, in a Publix on Folly Road.

Week 7, I had Cora over to my house on a Saturday. We made cookies. She told me a long story about a girl in her class named Mackenzie and a complicated incident involving a stolen sticker. I followed every detail. I asked her questions. I remembered the name of Mackenzie. I remembered the sticker was a unicorn. I remembered Cora had been on Mackenzie's side. I remembered the teacher's name.

A month earlier I would have lost the thread by the end of the story.

I did not lose the thread.

Week 10, Glenn looked at me one Sunday morning over the newspaper and he said, "Marlene. Something is different about you."

I said, "What do you mean."

He said, "I don't know. You've been sharper. You've been talking more. You don't trail off the way you have been."

I had not known I had been trailing off.

He had been watching it for longer than I had.

I told him that night, after dinner, what I had been doing. I told him about the recital. About the driveway. About the doctor. About the kitchen table at 2 AM. About the urolithin A. About Auniva.

He listened to all of it. He did not interrupt me. When I finished, he said, "Marlene. I have been worried about you for almost a year. I have not known how to bring it up."

We both cried at the kitchen table.

We have been married 38 years. We are not crying people. We had been hiding it from each other.

Week 12, I went to Cora's spring recital. Same Lutheran church on Camp Road. Same pew. Same program in my hand.

I sat there and I watched all 14 students play. I knew which one was Cora the entire time. I knew her teacher's name. I knew the name of the boy next to her, who was Eli still, and who was older now and not kicking the pew. I knew the names of the parents in the rows around me. I had brought yellow carnations this time, because Cora had told me last week she had decided yellow was her new favorite color.

A woman came up the aisle during intermission. Not the same woman as before. A different woman.

She said, "Excuse me, which one of these is yours."

I lifted my hand.

I pointed at Cora. I said, "She's the one in the front row in the lavender dress. Her name is Cora. She's playing 'Heart and Soul' today and she's been practicing it for 3 months."

The woman said, "Oh, isn't she lovely."

She walked away.

I sat there in that pew and I let myself feel what just happened.

Not a miracle. Not a cure. Just a brain that did its job. A drawer that opened when I asked it to open. A name that came when I called it.

I have been on Auniva Pomegranate for 8 months now.

I want to tell you what has stayed and what has not, because I do not want to mislead you.

What has stayed. The recall. The names. The plot points in the books I read. The thread of conversations with Cora. The word "sponge."

What has not. I still misplace my reading glasses. I still walk into rooms and forget why. I am still 59 years old and not 29 years old. I am not pretending I have my 29 year old brain back. I do not.

But the thing that was happening, the slow slipping, the pretending, the small private terror in the driveway, that has eased. The cellular housekeeping has been getting done. The drawer is opening when I ask it to open.

That is the thing I wanted back. That is what I have.

If you are 55 or 60 or 65 years old and you have been hiding the little moments from your husband, from your kids, from yourself, if you have been laughing them off and changing the subject and telling yourself it is fine, I want you to know it might not just be aging. It might be something specific. A specific thing inside your cells. A specific process that has slowed down and that might be supportable.

It was for me.

It might be for you.

I am not going to make you a big pitch. The thing speaks for itself or it doesn't. What I will say is for the price of a couple of those big lunches you do not really need, you can try a bottle. You take one capsule a day. You give it 8 weeks. If you notice something, you keep going. If you don't, you ship the bottle back within 90 days and they refund every penny. That is the whole deal. That is how Auniva stands behind it.

The link is below this story.

P.S. The 90 day guarantee is the part that mattered to me. Try it for up to 90 days. If it is not the right fit for you, send the bottle back for a full refund. That is the deal. You are not stuck. You try. If it is not for you, you send it back.

P.P.S. Cora's spring recital was 6 months ago. She has a fall recital coming up next Sunday. She is playing a Christmas song. She has been practicing it on Ashley's piano for 5 weeks. I have heard it roughly 200 times. I know every note. I know exactly when she is going to make her one little mistake. I know exactly when she is going to recover. I am bringing red carnations because she has decided red is her new favorite color and we are no longer in the yellow era. I will know that, on Sunday, because I have known her, all the way through, for 7 years.

P.P.P.S. I sat in my driveway for 22 minutes that day in March because I was scared of going inside and being alone with what I had just figured out about myself. I have not sat in that driveway since. I pull in. I get out. I go inside. The house is the same house. The woman walking into it is the woman I was scared was slipping away.

She did not slip away.

She just needed a little help from a fruit my grandmother Coralee used to buy at the farmer's market in McClellanville every fall.
