I pointed to the wrong child at my granddaughter's piano recital last March and I drove home in silence afterward and I sat in my own driveway for 22 minutes before I could make myself go inside the house.

That is where this story starts. Not in a hospital. Not in a doctor's office. In a Honda Civic in a driveway on James Island, South Carolina, with the engine off and my hands on the steering wheel and the late afternoon light coming through the windshield, trying to convince myself that what had just happened in that recital hall was not what I knew it was.

My name is Marlene. I'm 59 years old. I am a retired second grade teacher. I taught at the same elementary school in West Ashley for 28 years. I retired in 2021 because my husband Glenn had a heart scare and I wanted to be home more.

Glenn is fine now. Glenn is 63 and Glenn putters around the yard and Glenn drives me crazy in the kitchen and Glenn is exactly the man he has always been.

I am the one who is not exactly the woman I have always been.

I have one daughter, Ashley. Ashley is 34. Ashley lives 8 minutes from us in a little cottage off Folly Road with her husband Brett and their two kids. The oldest is my granddaughter Cora. Cora is 7. Cora has been taking piano lessons since she was 5 from a woman named Mrs. Pelletier who teaches out of her sun room in Riverland Terrace.

The recital was on a Sunday afternoon in March. 3 PM. At a Lutheran church on Camp Road that Mrs. Pelletier rents twice a year for these things. Glenn was out of town. He was in Greenville at his brother's lake house for the weekend doing some kind of fishing thing he does every year. So it was me, alone, in a pew, with a program in my hand and a bouquet of pink carnations on the seat next to me that I'd picked up from the Harris Teeter on the way over.

Cora was scheduled to play 9th, in the second half. She had been practicing "Annie's Song" by John Denver. She had been practicing it since January. I had heard it on Sunday afternoons at Ashley's house roughly 800 times.

The recital started. Children played. Parents clapped. There were 14 students that year, ranging from 5 years old to 12. They sat in the front three rows in little dresses and clip-on ties and patent leather shoes, waiting their turn.

The boy next to Cora was a kid named Eli, who was 8. He had blonde hair and a navy bow tie and he was kicking the back of the pew in front of him the entire first half of the recital and his mother kept reaching forward and putting a hand on his knee to make him stop.

I knew all of this. I had been watching all of it for 40 minutes.

We hit intermission. Mrs. Pelletier announced a 10 minute break. People got up to use the restroom and stretch their legs.

A woman I had never seen before came up the aisle and stopped at my pew. She was around my age. She was wearing a green blouse and reading glasses on a chain.

She smiled at me and she said, "Excuse me, I'm sorry to bother you, but I am here to see my niece play and I'm a little turned around. Which one of these little ones is yours?"

She was being friendly. She was making small talk. It was a totally ordinary moment in a totally ordinary church on a totally ordinary Sunday afternoon.

I lifted my hand and I pointed.

I pointed at a little girl in the third row in a yellow dress with brown hair in two French braids.

The woman said, "Oh, isn't she sweet."

She walked away.

I sat there with my finger half raised.

The little girl in the yellow dress with the brown hair in two French braids was not Cora.

Cora was in the front row.

Cora was in a navy blue dress with white piping. Her hair was down with a little pink ribbon in it. She was sitting right next to the kicking boy Eli.

The little girl in the yellow dress was a child I had never seen before in my life.

I had pointed at a stranger.

I had pointed at a stranger and identified her as my own granddaughter.

I had been watching Cora the entire first half. I had been watching Eli kick the pew next to her. I had been watching her play with the bow on her dress when she got nervous. And the second somebody asked me a simple question, my brain had reached into a drawer that was supposed to have Cora in it, and it had pulled out a stranger.

For 30 seconds.

For 30 seconds, I had pointed at the wrong child and called her mine.

I sat in that pew and I felt something cold move through my body that I have never felt before or since.

It was not embarrassment. The woman was gone. The woman did not know.

It was something deeper than embarrassment.

It was the feeling of finding out, in a single small moment, that the inside of you has been quietly slipping for longer than you have wanted to admit.

I made it through the rest of the recital. Cora played "Annie's Song" beautifully and made one tiny mistake at the bridge and recovered like a professional and I clapped and I cried a little, the way grandmas are supposed to cry, and I gave her the carnations and I hugged her and I told her I was so proud of her.

Ashley said, "Mama, you want to come back to the house? We're doing pizza."

I told her I had a headache. I told her I'd see them on Wednesday. I drove home.

I sat in my driveway for 22 minutes.

The thing is.

It wasn't the first time.

I had been pretending it was the first time. I had been pretending all the little moments before it didn't count. I had been pretending that the day I called Glenn by my father's name (my father has been dead since 2003) was a joke. That the time at the Publix when I couldn't remember the word "sponge" and stood in the cleaning aisle for 6 minutes trying to think of it was just because I was distracted. That the day I left my phone in the refrigerator next to the eggs was just because I was tired.

I had been pretending.

The recital broke the pretending.

I sat in that driveway and I let myself say the thing I had been refusing to say.

Something was happening to my brain.

Not in a dramatic way. Not in a hospital way. In a slow, quiet, terrifying way that I had been managing with humor and excuses for at least 2 years.

I knew what people my age were supposed to worry about. Everybody knows. We all have a friend whose mother went down that road. We all have an aunt who didn't recognize her own kids by the end. We all have a story we don't tell at parties.

I had been telling myself I was too young.

I am 59.

I am not too young for things to start shifting. I just had not been ready to admit they had started.

I sat in that driveway and I made myself a promise.

I was going to figure out what was happening to me.

Not because I was sure it was the worst thing. I was not sure. I am still not sure. I was going to figure out what was happening because the alternative, the pretending, the laughing it off, the calling Glenn by my father's name and shrugging, that was not a life I wanted to keep living.

I wanted to know what was actually going on.

I went inside the house. I made myself a cup of tea. I sat at the kitchen table.

I went to my doctor on Tuesday. I am going to tell you what happened at that appointment because I think a lot of women my age need to hear it.

I told her everything. The recital. The Publix sponge moment. Calling Glenn by my father's name. The phone in the refrigerator. The way I had been losing words mid sentence. The way I had been walking into rooms and forgetting why.

She listened. She was kind. She was 38 years old and she was kind.

She had me do a little test in the office. She asked me to count backwards from 100 by 7s. She asked me to remember three words. She asked me to draw a clock and put the hands at 10 past 11.

I did fine.

She told me I did fine.

She told me that what I was describing sounded like normal aging. She told me that everybody loses words sometimes. She told me that everybody puts the phone in weird places sometimes. She told me that pointing at the wrong child was likely just a brain hiccup, the kind anybody has when they get caught off guard.

She said, "Marlene, you're not in any cognitive danger zone right now. Your memory is going to be a little less sharp than it was at 35. That's normal."

I left her office with the same nothing I had walked in with.

She had been kind. She had been thorough. She had not lied to me.

But she had also not told me what was happening underneath the surface of my brain. She had told me I was fine. She had not told me why I, a woman who had memorized the names of 28 years of second graders, could not pull up the name of her own granddaughter when a stranger asked her at a piano recital.

I went home that Tuesday. I sat at the kitchen table again.

And for the first time in my life I did something I had spent my whole career as a teacher rolling my eyes at parents for doing.

I went on the internet to figure out what was wrong with me.

I sat at that kitchen table for 4 nights in a row after Glenn went to bed. I read until 1 AM. I read until 2 AM. I read with a notebook next to me and a pencil and I took notes the way I used to take notes when I was studying for my teaching certification in 1988.

I want to tell you what I found, because I think it matters.

I found out that inside every cell in your body, there are little structures called mitochondria. They are tiny. They are the part of your cells that produce energy. They are sometimes called the powerhouses of the cell.

I remembered that phrase from 7th grade science class. Powerhouses of the cell. I had taught that phrase to second graders in a unit on the human body. I had not thought about mitochondria once since 1992.

But the mitochondria are not just in the cells in your arms and legs. They are in the cells in your brain. They are in the neurons that fire when you remember a name. They are in the connections that pull a face out of a drawer when somebody asks you a question.

Your brain runs on mitochondria.

When you are young, your brain has plenty of healthy mitochondria. Your neurons fire clean and fast. You remember names. You pull words out without thinking. You watch a granddaughter for 40 minutes and you can point to her in a second.

But over the years, the mitochondria get worn down.

I sat at my kitchen table and I read this for the first time at 1 AM on a Wednesday in March and I cried a little.

Not from fear.

From recognition.

The mitochondria get worn down by stress. By poor sleep. By processed food. By environmental toxins. By aging itself. By 28 years of teaching second graders, which is a thing I am throwing in there for myself but which I believe to be biologically true.

Damaged mitochondria do not produce energy as cleanly. They start producing what the researchers called oxidative stress as a side product. Like a car with a worn out engine that starts coughing exhaust into its own cabin.

And the brain, of all the organs in your body, is the most demanding of clean mitochondrial energy. The brain uses about 20% of all the energy your body makes, even though it is only 2% of your body weight. When the mitochondria in your brain cells start sputtering, the brain feels it first.

Not in a dramatic way.

In a way that looks like pointing at the wrong child for 30 seconds.

In a way that looks like the word "sponge" not coming when you call it.

In a way that looks like calling your husband by your father's name.

I sat at that table and I felt every small moment of the last 2 years click into place.

This was not just aging. This was not just being 59. This was a specific thing happening inside the cells of my brain. A thing that had a name. A thing that researchers had been studying for decades. A thing that nobody, including the kind 38 year old doctor in her office on a Tuesday, had ever mentioned to me.

The next night I went back to the kitchen table and I kept reading.

I read about something called mitophagy. It is the word for the process the body uses to clean out damaged mitochondria and replace them with healthy ones. It is a thing your body does naturally. It is one of the body's most basic housekeeping functions.

But mitophagy slows down as you age. The damaged mitochondria stop getting cleared the way they used to. They pile up. They keep coughing exhaust into the cells. And the cells, especially the brain cells, suffer for it.

And then I read about a compound called urolithin A.

I had never heard of it.

Urolithin A, the article said, is a compound that researchers have been studying for its role in stimulating mitophagy. In helping the body do its housekeeping. In helping it clear out the damaged mitochondria and let the healthy ones do their job.

I read this very carefully. I read it twice. I am a retired teacher and I am not going to pretend I understood every word the first time.

The article said that urolithin A is produced in your gut, when your gut bacteria break down certain compounds you eat. The most studied source of those compounds, by a wide margin, is pomegranate.

Pomegranate.

The fruit my grandmother Coralee used to buy at the farmer's market in McClellanville every fall and eat at her kitchen table.

The article said that pomegranate contains compounds called punicalagins. Some of the most studied antioxidant compounds in all of nature. The article said pomegranate has one of the highest antioxidant profiles ever measured in a food. The article said ancient healers had called it the fruit of life for thousands of years and that there was a reason that name had stuck.

The punicalagins, when they get to your gut, are converted into urolithin A. The urolithin A then circulates through the body. And the research suggests it can help support the cellular housekeeping process that has been slowing down as you have been aging.

The damaged mitochondria can get cleared.

The cells, especially the brain cells, can run cleaner.

The body can do what it always knew how to do.

I sat at my kitchen table at 2:14 in the morning on a Thursday in March and I underlined that paragraph three times in my notebook.

I want to be very careful about how I describe what I felt next.

I did not feel like I had found a miracle. I am 59 years old and I have not believed in miracles since I was a child.

I felt like I had found a reasonable explanation for what was happening inside my body, and a reasonable thing to try that was not a prescription drug, that was not an injection, that was not a procedure, and that had research behind it going back decades.

That was all I had been looking for.

A reasonable explanation. A reasonable thing to try.

I kept reading. I read about a brand called Auniva.

I want to tell you why I chose them, because I am a careful woman with my money and I do not buy things on the internet without a reason.

Auniva did not promise me anything. They did not tell me their pomegranate was going to make me 30 again. They did not have a doctor in a white coat pointing at a brain scan. They explained the science. They explained the punicalagins. They explained what the research suggested and what it did not. They were honest about it in a way I had not seen on any of the other websites I had looked at.

And they backed every bottle with a 90 day money back guarantee. Which meant if it did not work for me, I could ship the bottle back inside 90 days and they would refund every penny.

That last part mattered. That meant I was not gambling. I was testing.

I ordered one bottle that Friday morning.

It came on a Wednesday.

I started that Thursday morning. One capsule with a glass of water before breakfast. I did not tell Glenn. I did not tell Ashley. I did not tell anybody. I wanted to see what happened without anybody watching me for it.

I want to tell you what happened over the next 12 weeks, and I want you to know I am not exaggerating any of it.

Week 1, nothing. I expected nothing. The article had said the process is slow because the cellular housekeeping takes time.

Week 2, nothing I could put my finger on. I was waiting for something dramatic. I did not get it.

Week 3, I noticed something small. I was reading a novel one night before bed and I realized I had read 40 pages and I could remember every plot point. I had been struggling to remember what I had read by morning for at least a year. I had been blaming the books. I had been telling myself I was picking boring ones.

It had not been the books.

Week 5, I was at the Publix and I was in the cleaning aisle. I caught myself.

I was in the cleaning aisle and I had walked there on purpose to buy sponges. I had remembered the word. I had remembered it without searching for it. I had walked in, gone to the aisle, picked up the sponges, and put them in my cart.

I stood there with the sponges in my hand for a minute and I just laughed, quietly, by myself, in a Publix on Folly Road.

Week 7, I had Cora over to my house on a Saturday. We made cookies. She told me a long story about a girl in her class named Mackenzie and a complicated incident involving a stolen sticker. I followed every detail. I asked her questions. I remembered the name of Mackenzie. I remembered the sticker was a unicorn. I remembered Cora had been on Mackenzie's side. I remembered the teacher's name.

A month earlier I would have lost the thread by the end of the story.

I did not lose the thread.

Week 10, Glenn looked at me one Sunday morning over the newspaper and he said, "Marlene. Something is different about you."

I said, "What do you mean."

He said, "I don't know. You've been sharper. You've been talking more. You don't trail off the way you have been."

I had not known I had been trailing off.

He had been watching it for longer than I had.

I told him that night, after dinner, what I had been doing. I told him about the recital. About the driveway. About the doctor. About the kitchen table at 2 AM. About the urolithin A. About Auniva.

He listened to all of it. He did not interrupt me. When I finished, he said, "Marlene. I have been worried about you for almost a year. I have not known how to bring it up."

We both cried at the kitchen table.

We have been married 38 years. We are not crying people. We had been hiding it from each other.

Week 12, I went to Cora's spring recital. Same Lutheran church on Camp Road. Same pew. Same program in my hand.

I sat there and I watched all 14 students play. I knew which one was Cora the entire time. I knew her teacher's name. I knew the name of the boy next to her, who was Eli still, and who was older now and not kicking the pew. I knew the names of the parents in the rows around me. I had brought yellow carnations this time, because Cora had told me last week she had decided yellow was her new favorite color.

A woman came up the aisle during intermission. Not the same woman as before. A different woman.

She said, "Excuse me, which one of these is yours."

I lifted my hand.

I pointed at Cora. I said, "She's the one in the front row in the lavender dress. Her name is Cora. She's playing 'Heart and Soul' today and she's been practicing it for 3 months."

The woman said, "Oh, isn't she lovely."

She walked away.

I sat there in that pew and I let myself feel what just happened.

Not a miracle. Not a cure. Just a brain that did its job. A drawer that opened when I asked it to open. A name that came when I called it.

I have been on Auniva Pomegranate for 8 months now.

I want to tell you what has stayed and what has not, because I do not want to mislead you.

What has stayed. The recall. The names. The plot points in the books I read. The thread of conversations with Cora. The word "sponge."

What has not. I still misplace my reading glasses. I still walk into rooms and forget why. I am still 59 years old and not 29 years old. I am not pretending I have my 29 year old brain back. I do not.

But the thing that was happening, the slow slipping, the pretending, the small private terror in the driveway, that has eased. The cellular housekeeping has been getting done. The drawer is opening when I ask it to open.

That is the thing I wanted back. That is what I have.

If you are 55 or 60 or 65 years old and you have been hiding the little moments from your husband, from your kids, from yourself, if you have been laughing them off and changing the subject and telling yourself it is fine, I want you to know it might not just be aging. It might be something specific. A specific thing inside your cells. A specific process that has slowed down and that might be supportable.

It was for me.

It might be for you.

I am not going to make you a big pitch. The thing speaks for itself or it doesn't. What I will say is for the price of a couple of those big lunches you do not really need, you can try a bottle. P.P.S. Cora's spring recital was 6 months ago. She has a fall recital coming up next Sunday. She is playing a Christmas song. She has been practicing it on Ashley's piano for 5 weeks. I have heard it roughly 200 times. I know every note. I know exactly when she is going to make her one little mistake. I know exactly when she is going to recover. I am bringing red carnations because she has decided red is her new favorite color and we are no longer in the yellow era. I had been constipated for three days when my daughter followed me into the bathroom at my birthday dinner.

She thought I was sick.

Then my purse hit the floor.

Miralax packets, magnesium capsules, Dulcolax, and my emergency pouch spilled across the tile.

She looked down at all of it and asked, "Mom... is all of this for tonight?"

I said no before I could stop myself.

"No. This is just what I carry."

My name is Elaine.

I'm 55 years old.

I work part-time at the front desk of a dental office in New Haven.

I have one daughter, Megan, who is 29 and has always believed I am more put-together than I am.

I have been married to my husband Robert for 31 years.

From the outside, my life looks ordinary.

Good ordinary.

The kind of ordinary I used to be proud of.

But for the last seven years, the most important thing in my purse has not been my wallet.

It has been that pouch.

If any of what I describe sounds familiar to you, please don't stop reading until you get to the part about the doctor.

Because she told me something I needed to hear seven years ago.

She told me something I think you need to hear right now.

Especially if you have been on Miralax or magnesium or anything stronger for more than a year, and you still tell yourself it is just a normal morning routine because your doctor said it was safe.

And especially if you have ever hidden how much you carry, how much you take, or how much you plan around the bathroom.

Because the shame was not the diagnosis.

That is what I did not understand yet.

I want to start with the dinner.

It was a Saturday in May.

My birthday.

Megan had made the reservation herself because she said I never let anyone make a fuss over me.

Megan had driven forty minutes to meet us there.

It was one of those Italian restaurants with low lighting and framed family photos on the walls.

Robert ordered the chicken marsala.

Megan ordered the salmon.

I ordered pasta because it was my birthday and I wanted to act like a normal person.

For the first half hour, I did a decent job.

I smiled.

I opened the card.

I told Megan I loved the earrings.

I said I was fine when Robert asked why I had barely touched the bread.

That was the word I used most back then.

Fine.

My stomach was hard under the waistband of my pants.

I had not gone in three days.

I had taken Miralax that morning.

Magnesium the night before.

Dulcolax at 11 PM.

Nothing.

But my daughter had driven forty minutes to take me to dinner, and I was not going to ruin the night by becoming the kind of mother people had to worry about.

Halfway through the meal, I excused myself to the bathroom.

I told them I wanted to check my lipstick.

That was not completely a lie.

In the stall, I sat there with my elbows on my knees, doing the math.

If I took another Dulcolax when I got home, would it hit before morning?

If I added magnesium too, would I cramp all night?

If I did nothing, would this become four days?

Then I heard Megan's voice outside the stall.

"Mom?"

I said, "I'm fine."

She said, "You keep saying that."

I came out too quickly.

My purse slipped off my shoulder.

It hit the floor.

The zipper was open.

The pouch slid out and spilled across the tile.

Three Miralax packets.

The magnesium case.

The Dulcolax.

The emergency things I had sworn I would never need unless things got truly bad.

Everything I had been carrying like a secret second bathroom.

Megan bent down to help me pick it up.

Then she stopped.

That was when she asked:

"Mom... is all of this for tonight?"

I wanted to lie.

I wanted to say I was traveling after dinner.

I wanted to say it was old.

I wanted to say she was overreacting.

Instead I heard myself say:

"No. This is just what I carry."

She did not yell.

That almost made it worse.

She just looked scared.

Not disgusted.

Not angry.

Scared.

Like she had just realized there was a whole part of my life she had not been allowed to see.

We went back to the table.

I said I had a headache.

Megan asked for the check.

Robert drove us home.

No one ordered dessert.

That night did not diagnose me.

It exposed me.

There is a difference.

I want to tell you how I got there, but I will keep it short, because the way you got here is probably similar.

I turned 48 in the summer of 2018.

My periods stopped that fall.

A few months after that, I noticed I was not going to the bathroom every day anymore.

Then every other day.

Then twice a week.

I went to my GP, a man who had been my doctor since I was 30.

He said, and I am quoting him: "Try a capful of Miralax in your morning coffee. It's totally safe. Doesn't cause any issues. You can take it as long as you need to."

I trusted him.

I went home and started taking it.

I was 48 years old.

For about a year, it worked.

A capful in the morning, by ten o'clock my body would do what it was supposed to do, and I would forget about it for the rest of the day.

Then it stopped feeling reliable.

At first, that did not mean some dramatic failure.

It meant I started thinking about timing.

It meant I kept checking whether I had enough left in the bottle.

It meant I felt uneasy on mornings when nothing happened by ten.

And eventually, for me, it meant I went to two capfuls.

Then I added magnesium powder at night, mixed in water.

Then on the bad weeks I started taking Dulcolax.

Then there were not really good weeks anymore, just less-bad ones.

By the summer I turned 54, I was on Miralax in the morning, magnesium at night, and Dulcolax three or four times a week.

That summer was when the pouch started.

At first, it was one packet.

Just in case.

Then two.

Then magnesium.

Then Dulcolax.

Then the emergency items I told myself I would never use unless things got truly bad.

The pouch made me feel prepared.

That is the lie I told myself.

What it really did was let me keep pretending this was private.

Megan thought my bloating was diet.

Robert thought I was anxious.

My GP thought it was benign chronic constipation.

Everyone had a theory.

Nobody asked whether my body could still start on its own.

Up until that year, I had been telling myself a story.

The story was: this is a problem I am managing, like blood pressure, like cholesterol.

I take my scoop, my body works, life continues.

That story stopped being available to me after my daughter saw the pouch.

And I want to tell you exactly when it broke.

It was 2 AM, three nights after my birthday dinner.

Robert was asleep next to me.

I had taken my normal evening doses six hours earlier.

Nothing had happened.

I had been bloated all day.

I had taken an extra Dulcolax at 11 PM out of panic.

Still nothing.

I remember lying there and thinking, if I am carrying half a pharmacy in my purse, what happens when even that stops working?

That was the sentence that made me pick up my phone.

First I searched, "can laxatives make your colon stop working."

That was when I saw the phrase that made my stomach drop.

Cathartic colon.

I typed the words "cathartic colon."

If you do not know what cathartic colon is, do not Google it tonight.

Read the rest of this first.

Because what I read at 2 AM that night was the beginning of the worst year or so of my life.

Cathartic colon, in the way it gets described online, in old medical literature, on the threads I read, is what happens when your colon has been chemically pushed for so long that it stops answering.

The muscles stop contracting.

The colon goes dead.

And the only treatment, the women writing online said, was surgery.

A partial colectomy.

They take the dead section out and reconnect what is left.

Some women in those threads had had this done at 60.

Some at 55.

Some at 48.

I sat in bed and read every single thread I could find, and then the page after that, and then the page after that.

I read women describing recoveries.

I read women describing complications.

I read one woman, and I will not forget this for the rest of my life, describing what it is like to live with a permanent colostomy bag at 52.

A colostomy bag is a pouch attached to an opening in your abdomen so stool can leave your body into the bag instead of through your rectum.

I had known the words before.

I had never pictured them happening to me.

She wrote about learning how to empty the pouch without looking down for too long.

She wrote about planning clothes around whether the outline would show.

She wrote about checking for leaks before leaving the house.

She wrote about worrying about odor in a quiet room.

She wrote about lying beside her husband and feeling like there was a part of her body she could no longer keep private.

And all I could think was: if I kept forcing my colon every day, was that where this ended?

I closed my phone at 4:30 AM.

I did not sleep.

That night did not really leave me for the next twelve months.

Every dose I took, I thought about it.

Every time the dose did not work, I thought about it harder.

Every time I zipped the pouch, I thought about Megan's face on the bathroom floor.

I started checking my abdomen in the mirror obsessively, looking for distortion, looking for hardness, looking for the shape of something that had stopped working.

Once, that fall, I tried to stop.

Cold turkey.

I made it three days before I had gained six pounds of water weight and could not button a single pair of pants I owned.

I went back on the Miralax.

I never tried again.

I made an appointment with my GP, the one who had put me on Miralax seven years before.

I told him I was scared I had damaged myself.

He looked at my chart.

He said: "Your bloodwork looks fine. You had a colonoscopy at 50, that was clean. You're okay. Just keep doing what you're doing. We don't really have great options for chronic constipation."

This was not the answer that changed everything.

This was the appointment that made me realize no one had answered the thing I was actually afraid of.

I drove home from that appointment crying.

Not because he had been mean.

Because he had not.

He had been kind, and he had told me there was nothing else.

He had basically told me this was just my life now.

The Miralax.

The bottle in the cabinet.

The backup scoop in my travel bag.

The extra packet in my purse.

The quiet inventory check before every overnight trip.

The calculation before every dinner.

The question of whether I should take more now or risk paying for it later.

The fear that every missed morning would become two missed mornings.

The knowledge that no matter how carefully I hid the routine, the routine was still in charge.

All of it.

Forever.

It felt less like a treatment plan than a sentence.

And I had no idea how many years I was supposed to serve.

I want to skip ahead now, to the following May, to the day everything changed.

It was a Wednesday in May.

I had taken my full evening stack the night before, magnesium powder and two Dulcolax, and woken up Tuesday morning to nothing.

I had added another capful of Miralax Tuesday morning.

Nothing.

By Tuesday evening I was so bloated I could not button my work pants.

I took an extra Dulcolax Tuesday night.

Nothing.

Wednesday morning I woke up at 5:30 and lay in bed with my hand on my stomach, and I could feel it.

It was hard.

It was distended.

It had not moved in four days despite everything I had thrown at it.

And the thought that came into my head, lying there in the dark, was: this is it.

This is the day my body finally stopped responding.

I have killed it.

I told Robert I needed to go to urgent care.

He offered to come with me.

I told him no.

I did not want him to see what was about to happen.

I did not want him sitting beside me while a stranger opened my chart and saw the whole thing.

I drove myself to the urgent care on Farmington Avenue.

I sat in the waiting room for an hour and a half.

When the doctor saw me, a woman maybe in her forties, in scrubs, tired, I told her I thought I had an obstruction.

I told her about the seven years.

I told her about the doses.

I told her I had not had a bowel movement in four days despite every laxative I owned.

She sent me for an abdominal X-ray.

I waited another forty minutes.

She came back into the exam room with the result on a tablet.

She turned the screen toward me.

She said, "There's no obstruction. You have a significant amount of stool throughout your colon, but no obstruction. Your colon is just being sluggish today. I'd recommend a stronger dose tonight. Maybe try an enema if it's not moving by tomorrow."

I sat on the exam table and stared at her.

I had been preparing, for an hour and a half in the waiting room, for her to tell me my colon was dead.

I had been preparing for surgery.

I had been preparing for the worst.

What she told me was almost worse.

She had told me nothing was wrong.

That what I was experiencing, the bloat, the not-going, the four days of nothing, was just my normal now.

That I should take more.

I drove from the urgent care to an empty parking lot and sat in my car for forty-five minutes and cried.

This is what I want every woman reading this to understand.

I was not crying because I was sick.

I was crying because no one in medicine was going to help me.

I had been to my GP, who told me I was fine.

I had been to an urgent care, who told me to take more.

I had had a colonoscopy at 50 that came back clean.

I had had bloodwork that came back clean.

The system had nothing else to offer me.

And I was certain, in a way I had been certain for almost a year, that I had broken something inside me that was not going to come back, and I was going to have to live with it.

I went home.

I told Robert what had happened.

He sat down on the couch next to me and held my hand and said:

"There has to be a doctor somewhere who treats this. There has to be a specialist. Let's find one."

So we started searching.

What I learned in the days that followed is that most gastroenterologists treat structural problems, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, polyps, cancer screening, hemorrhoids.

There is a smaller subspecialty within gastroenterology called motility.

Motility doctors focus on how the gut moves, rather than what it looks like.

Most major university hospitals have one or two motility specialists on staff.

Most regional hospitals have none.

The first thing I learned was how rare they are.

The second thing I learned was how hard they can be to get in front of.

The offices we called were booked out for months.

Some required referrals.

Some did not take new patients.

Some consultations were the kind of expensive that makes you put the phone down and stare at the wall for a minute.

Even with insurance, I could see why most women would stop looking right there.

The one Robert found was Dr. Karen Mitchell.

She had completed her gastroenterology training at the Cleveland Clinic in the 1990s and stayed there for the first decade of her career doing research on the bacterial ecology of the human colon.

She moved to Connecticut in 2012 to build the motility program at the university hospital here.

Her clinic was eight weeks out for new patients.

She did not advertise.

She took referrals only from primary care physicians or other gastroenterologists.

Robert got my GP to write the referral letter the day after I came home from urgent care.

The reason we found her at all was that a woman in Robert's office had a sister-in-law who had been her patient three years earlier and would not stop talking about her.

That is how rare this kind of doctor is.

The eight weeks of waiting were ordinary.

I did what I had been doing for seven years.

I want to take you to the morning of the appointment.

It was a Tuesday in July.

I had myself fully prepared for what Dr. Mitchell was going to tell me.

I had Googled "cathartic colon" probably a hundred more times in the eight-week wait.

I was convinced she was going to look at my chart, run a test, and tell me my colon was structurally damaged.

That maybe I would need surgery in five years.

That I had done this to myself and now I had to live with it.

I went in expecting the death sentence I had been preparing for since the previous July.

The waiting room had a poster about colon cancer awareness on one wall and a fake plant in the corner.

When she walked into the exam room, the first thing I noticed was that she was about my age.

Late fifties.

Short gray hair.

Wire-rimmed glasses.

She sat down on the rolling stool, opened her laptop, and read my chart in silence for almost two full minutes.

Then she looked up at me and asked:

"When was the last time you had a bowel movement without taking anything?"

I sat there trying to count back.

I could not.

The honest answer was I genuinely could not remember the last time my body had done that on its own.

She watched me try to count, and then she said, very quietly:

"It's okay. I want you to know that I see this pattern every single week, multiple times a week. Women your age. Women younger than you. You are not unusual. And you are not broken in the way you think you are."

I started crying right there in the exam room.

I had spent a year preparing for the opposite sentence.

She handed me a tissue and she waited.

Then she said: "I want to run one test on you today, just to confirm severity. But I want you to understand something before I do."

She said: "I have already heard enough from you to know what's going on. The test won't change my diagnosis. It'll only tell me how far along it is."

She ordered a sitz marker test.

You swallow a capsule containing 24 small radio-opaque markers, and they take X-rays at 24, 48, and 72 hours to see how many have moved through your system.

The point was to give my colon's movement a number by showing how many markers were still stuck after 72 hours.

It also was not the kind of test I could have casually ordered for myself the first night I panicked.

It was a specialist-ordered, multi-visit imaging test.

Exactly the kind of thing that can turn into a very expensive bill fast.

So when she ordered it, I understood why most women never get this far.

"Come back in three weeks. We'll go over the result."

Three weeks later I was back.

She came in with a folder and sat down and said, "I want to walk you through what's been happening to you. And I'm going to take some time with this. Because nobody has probably explained it to you this way before."

Here is what she told me.

I am going to do my best to reproduce it the way she said it, because I have replayed this conversation in my head a hundred times since.

She started by drawing a circle on a notepad.

"This is your colon."

She drew a wavy line across the inside of the circle.

"Inside your colon, you have an entire ecosystem. Trillions of bacteria, fungi, archaea. Most of them are beneficial. They digest your food, regulate your immune system, produce vitamins, and tell your colon muscles when to contract."

She paused.

"In a healthy gut, the good bacteria outnumber the bad ones by a huge margin. The bad ones are still there, but they're crowded out, kept in check, and they can't really establish themselves."

She drew a few small dots inside the circle.

"In a gut like yours, and I see hundreds of these every year, the worker bacteria that help run the rhythm have thinned out. The pattern you're describing to me, the dose-stacking, the progressive failure of every laxative class, the bloating pattern, that's almost always one specific thing. Your colon is intact. The signal has gone quiet."

I asked her what that meant.

"It means your colon muscles are still there. The nerves are still there. But the little chemical messages that tell the muscle to move are not arriving the way they should."

She made a fist and slowly opened it.

"This is what your colon muscles should do, contract, relax, contract, relax. That's called peristalsis. It's what moves food through your intestines."

She held her fist closed.

"When the signal gets weak, the muscle doesn't fire normally. The colon doesn't go dead. It goes quiet. Your body is not damaged in the way you think. It's being under-signaled. Chemically. By what's missing from that ecosystem."

I had to ask her to slow down.

She did.

She said: "Your sitz marker test showed you retained 21 of 24 markers at 72 hours. That puts you in the severe slow-transit category. Most healthy adults retain fewer than five at 72 hours."

I knew the number was bad.

Hearing her say it made me feel sick.

"Here's what's happened over the last seven years. Every time you've taken a stimulant laxative, your Dulcolax, it whips the muscles into a contraction. You get a bowel movement. But it doesn't rebuild the signal. The signal stays quiet."

She paused.

"And every time you've taken Miralax, you've drawn water into the colon and forced material through. Again, you may get through today. But the rhythm that should run tomorrow does not come back."

Another pause.

"And every round of magnesium you've ever taken? The reason it stopped working is because your colon adapted. The worker population didn't rebuild. The signal just kept getting quieter."

I asked her the question I had asked four doctors over seven years:

"Why couldn't anyone else see this?"

She gave me a tired smile.

"Because we don't think about it this way in mainstream gastroenterology. The standard workup looks at structure. Your colonoscopy looked at the walls of your colon, which were normal. Your bloodwork looked for warning signs, which were normal. But neither one looked at whether the rhythm was being properly signaled."

She said: "Most of us were trained to ask, is there a blockage, inflammation, bleeding, cancer, something visible?"

She said: "We were not trained to ask, can this colon still initiate movement without being pushed?"

Then she said the thing I want every woman reading this to hear.

I want you to read it twice if you have to.

She said: "What you have is real. It is diagnosable. And it is reversible. You have not destroyed your colon. You have a quiet-signal problem."

"Your colon isn't dead. The signal has gone quiet."

I am not going to pretend I did not sob.

I had spent a year in a private hell of believing I had broken something inside my body that could not be repaired.

A year of 2 AM Googling.

A year of looking at my abdomen in the mirror and seeing a body I had ruined.

A year of preparing for surgery.

And in one sentence, a doctor I had known for 25 minutes had taken all of it back.

Then she said: "But I have to tell you the rest of it. Because the part you haven't heard yet is the most important."

She said: "The reason your body hasn't rebuilt that rhythm, even after everything you've thrown at it, and I do mean everything, is that the bacteria involved in that signal need to be fed."

She tapped the notepad.

She said there is a short-chain fatty acid called butyrate.

It is one of the go-signals that helps tell the colon muscle to contract.

Certain beneficial bacteria in the colon lining produce it.

Those bacteria do not come back just because you keep forcing water through with a scoop.

"They need food."

"Very specific food."

I asked her what kind.

She said: "There is a group of dark plant pigments called anthocyanins. They're what give certain plants that deep red, purple, almost ruby color. And in the colon, those pigments can feed the bacteria that help produce the signal."

She must have seen my face, because she smiled.

She said: "I know how this sounds. I know, believe me, I know how this sounds. I'm a board-certified gastroenterologist. I spent twenty years prescribing prokinetics. I would have laughed at this in 2012."

She said the difference was the literature.

She named the research on hibiscus anthocyanins, microbiome diversity, beneficial bacteria, and butyrate production.

I did not understand every study she mentioned.

I am not going to pretend I did.

What I understood was the part I could not stop repeating in my head.

The scoop had been helping me get through a morning.

But it had never been feeding the part of me that was supposed to make mornings work again.

That is what I could not stop thinking about.

Seven years of forcing today's load.

Seven years of never rebuilding tomorrow's rhythm.

I asked her what we do about it.

She said: "Three things have to happen. In this exact order."

She held up one finger.

"First, you have to feed the bacteria involved in the signal."

Second finger.

"Then you have to do it consistently enough that the rhythm has a chance to come back."

Third finger.

"And you have to do it gently, without turning your morning into another emergency."

She looked at me.

"Stimulants fail the third step. They can force a movement, but they can also create cramps, urgency, and more fear."

"Osmotic laxatives fail the first step. They move water. They do not feed the signal."

"That is where Miralax falls."

"It may help you get through today, but it does not feed the bacteria involved in natural bowel movements."

"Most probiotics fail because they are not food for the bacteria already living in your colon lining. You're throwing seeds onto ground you haven't fed."

She paused.

"There are not many everyday foods that deliver the right pigments in a form most women will actually use every day."

Then she told me about whole hibiscus flowers.

Not hibiscus flavor.

Not a red tea bag.

Whole hibiscus flowers.

She said the deep ruby pigment is the point.

She said the darker the flower, the more of those anthocyanins it tends to carry.

She said the flowers have to be grown, picked, dried, and kept in a way that preserves that pigment.

She said if the hibiscus is crushed into dust, blended with other herbs, or sitting in a weak little tea bag, the cup can look red and still not be the ingredient the research successfully used.

I asked her where you get the right kind.

She laughed and said, "This is where it gets interesting."

"This is the part most people get wrong."

She said she did not care what brand I bought yet, as long as it was true whole-flower hibiscus with deep pigment.

She said whole hibiscus flowers were the point.

Not hibiscus flavor.

Not a red tea bag.

Whole flowers.

She said the flowers had to stay intact enough to carry the dark pigment into the cup.

She said most cheaper hibiscus teas were made for flavor and color.

Not for delivering enough intact plant pigment to make a daily digestive ritual worth doing.

I thought I understood.

What I heard was hibiscus.

I wish someone had stopped me right there, because the next thing I did was exactly what you may be tempted to do.

Then I asked the question that had been building in my throat for an hour.

"Do I have to stop the Miralax?"

This is the part I want every woman reading this to underline.

Because I know this fear.

I knew it even more after Megan saw the pouch.

Part of me wanted to go home and throw the whole thing away just so I would not have to be the woman carrying it anymore.

The thought of stopping cold turkey was, in some ways, more terrifying than anything she had said up to this point.

I had tried, the previous fall, and I had made it three days.

She said: "Absolutely not. You keep taking your Miralax. We do not change anything in your current protocol on day one."

Then she said the sentence I needed more than I knew.

"Do not stop because you're embarrassed. That creates another emergency."

"Keep the pouch for now. We are not taking away your emergency exit on day one."

She said: "Here's what's going to happen."

"You're going to start whole hibiscus flowers."

"Two servings a day."

"One deep ruby serving in the morning."

"One more after dinner."

"You continue everything else as normal."

"Over the first three to four weeks, as the bacteria get fed and the signal starts to come back online, your own motility will start to come back online."

"As it does, and you will feel this, you will naturally need less and less Miralax."

"Your body will tell you."

"We don't taper on a schedule."

"We taper on response."

I started crying again.

I had not realized, until that moment, how badly I needed somebody to tell me I did not have to choose between the laxatives that had broken my body and the shame of being seen with them.

That I could keep my safety net.

That my body would be the one to tell me when to put it down.

She walked me out.

It was a sunny Tuesday in July.

I sat in my car in the parking garage for almost forty minutes before I drove home.

I had walked into that office with a year of fear sitting in my chest.

I walked out with a different sentence in my head than the one I had been carrying since the previous July.

But I want to be honest about something I did wrong first.

Because this is the part that almost made me think the whole thing was nonsense.

The next morning, I went to the grocery store.

The tea aisle had three kinds of hibiscus.

A red box with a flower on it.

A blended herbal tea.

The store brand.

I bought the familiar red box because it was $3.79 and it said hibiscus on the front.

I started drinking it the way she told me to: two cups a day.

One in the morning.

One after dinner.

Week one on the grocery tea: still one scoop in my coffee.

Still no morning rhythm.

Week three on the grocery tea: the same cramping.

The same hard pressure under my ribs.

The same careful calculations before dinner out with Robert and Megan.

Something had to be wrong.

Six weeks later, I was sitting at the kitchen table with the empty box beside me.

I turned it over and read the ingredients again.

Hibiscus.

Rosehips.

Lemongrass.

Peppermint.

Natural flavor.

That was the part I could not ignore.

I had bought a tea that happened to contain hibiscus.

I had not bought the thing Dr. Mitchell had actually described.

She had described whole flowers carrying deep pigment.

I had bought a blend in a paper tea bag.

That night, I pulled up the notes from her office again.

I wanted to know exactly what kind of hibiscus she had told me to look for.

That was when I saw the words I had skipped past.

Whole flower.

Deep pigment.

Carefully dried.

The anthocyanins were the point.

Not flavor.

Not a pretty red tea bag.

The intact flowers had to carry enough of the dark pigment to be worth doing every day.

Then I understood the delivery problem.

Most grocery-store hibiscus was broken petals and dust.

Blended with other herbs.

Crushed into tea bags and left on shelves because it made a cheap, red cup of tea.

But crushing the flower exposed more surface area.

Heat, air, and time took more of the pigment away.

By the time a lot of grocery-store hibiscus reached your cup, you were drinking red water with a memory of the flower that was supposed to do the work.

It was not that hibiscus did not work.

It was that I had bought the version with none of the qualities Dr. Mitchell had told me to look for.

High-altitude growing mattered because the flowers had to make more of that protective pigment under stronger sun.

Hand-picking mattered because the deepest-red flowers could be chosen at their peak instead of stripped for volume.

Careful drying mattered because the pigment is fragile.

Keeping the flowers whole mattered because dust and fragments can lose the very compounds you are trying to preserve.

That was the difference I had missed when I grabbed the $3.79 box.

But I found one company making a whole-flower tea that matched what she had been talking about.

PiPi Tea.

Organic whole hibiscus flowers.

High-altitude grown.

Hand-picked.

Carefully dried.

Deep ruby flowers, not dusty fragments swept into a tea bag.

The thing that made me trust them was not just that they sold hibiscus.

Everyone sells hibiscus.

It was that their entire product was built around the same details Dr. Mitchell had told me to look for.

Whole flowers.

Deep pigment.

No dusty blends.

No "hibiscus flavor."

No weak tea bag pretending color was the same thing as substance.

When the bag arrived, I could actually see the difference.

The flowers were still there.

Not hidden inside a paper bag as red powder.

Whole, dark, ruby pieces that made the grocery-store tea look like a shortcut.

I read the reviews.

Women describing exactly what I was going through.

Years of Miralax that never restored their rhythm.

Then, within weeks, mornings when they could finally go on their own.

I ordered a bag at 3:15 AM.

When it arrived, I started immediately.

I want to tell you what happened next, but I want to be honest with you about the first three weeks.

Because this is the part where people give up.

Week one on PiPi Tea: nothing dramatic.

I felt about the same.

I drank two servings of PiPi Tea every day, one in the morning, one after dinner.

I kept the Miralax.

I kept the pouch as a safety net.

I waited.

The only thing I noticed in week one was that my bathroom trips were maybe, maybe, slightly less effortful.

Week two: I woke up one morning and my stomach was flat.

Not bikini-flat.

Normal-flat.

The way mine used to be when I was 47.

I stood in front of the mirror and stared at it.

Then I did something I had not done in seven years.

I went downstairs, made coffee, and did not add the Miralax to it.

I just wanted to see what would happen.

At 9:15 AM, on my own, with no chemical assistance, I had a real bowel movement.

I sat there afterwards and cried for ten minutes.

I texted Robert.

I just said, "I went on my own."

He wrote back, "Honey."

That is the whole text.

Just: honey.

Week three: I had three unassisted bowel movements that week.

The bloating was noticeably down by mid-afternoon.

I cut the Miralax to half a capful in the morning, just as a hedge.

I still carried the pouch.

But I did not open it as much.

Week four: I started forgetting my magnesium.

By the time I would remember, it was 10 PM and I would think, well, let's see what happens if I don't take it.

The next morning, on my own, I went.

Around week five something happened that I did not connect to any of this until later.

When Megan suggested going back to the same restaurant, I almost said no.

Megan and Robert took me back to the same restaurant.

Same low lighting.

Same framed family photos.

Same bathroom hallway.

Only this time, I did not excuse myself halfway through the meal.

I did not scan for the bathroom when we sat down.

I did not touch the pouch in my purse.

I ate the pasta.

I stayed at the table.

When dessert came, Megan looked at me and said:

"You stayed at the table the whole time."

I wanted to laugh it off.

Instead I said, "I know."

And then both of us had tears in our eyes.

Week six: I had not taken Miralax in nine days.

I had not taken magnesium in eleven days.

I had not taken Dulcolax in over a month.

Week eight: I cleaned out my purse.

I found the pouch in the inside pocket.

Still zipped.

I had carried it for two weeks without opening it.

I did not throw it away.

Not yet.

But I moved it from my purse to the bathroom cabinet.

That probably sounds small.

It was not small to me.

For years, that pouch had been proof that I could not leave the house without backup.

That day, for the first time, it felt like backup again.

Not my life.

Not something I had to carry into every room.

Month six: I went back to see Dr. Mitchell for a follow-up sitz marker.

I retained 4 of 24 markers at 72 hours.

Down from 21.

She showed me the comparison on her laptop and shook her head slowly and said, "This is what your colon looks like when you let it work."

body:
I forgot a woman's name at the Publix on Forest Drive and sat in my car for 10 minutes afterward.

It was a Wednesday morning, around 10:30, and I was in the produce section pinching avocados the way my mother taught me to. I had my list in my pocket. I had nowhere to be. I was the most relaxed I'd been all week, and that's the part that's important, because what happened next happened to a relaxed woman in good spirits, which is not the version of me you'd expect to fall apart.

A voice said, "Patricia."

I turned around.

The woman was in her mid 40s. Blonde hair pulled back. Cream colored cardigan. A toddler in the cart who had to be a grandchild, because she was too put together for a young mother and her face had that 40-something softness.

She said my name like we were friends.

She smiled at me the way you smile at somebody you've shared something with. She said, "Oh my goodness, it's been so long. How are you?" And she came around the avocado bin with her arms half open, the way somebody does when they're going in for the hug but they're checking to see if you want one too.

And I stood there with an avocado in my hand and I had absolutely no idea who she was.

I knew I knew her. I knew it deep in some part of me that wasn't connecting to whatever part is supposed to know names. Her face was familiar in a way that made it worse. If she'd been a total stranger I could have just said, "I'm sorry, I think you have me confused with someone else." But I knew her. We had history. And the history was just gone.

I did what you do.

I hugged her. I said, "Oh my goodness, it's been forever. How are you?" I asked about her, generally, in the kind of vague way you can ask without giving anything away. She told me her oldest had gotten into Clemson. I made the appropriate sounds. She told me she'd retired from the district 2 years ago. I felt something cold move down my back, because if she'd been with the district, I had almost certainly known her name as well as I knew the names of my own children.

She talked for about 4 minutes. I nodded. I smiled. I asked about her husband, generically. She told me about her husband, whose name I also did not retrieve. She told me about a vacation they were taking. She said she'd been meaning to call me. She said we should get coffee.

And then she said, "Well, I'll let you finish your shopping. So good to see you, Patricia."

She hugged me again. She wheeled her cart away. The toddler waved at me over her shoulder.

I stood there with the avocado in my hand.

I put it in my cart. I picked up a different one. I put that one in my cart too. I walked over to the bananas. I stood by the bananas for what felt like 2 minutes. My heart was going. My hands had that buzzing feeling you get when you've had too much coffee.

I left my cart there.

I walked out of the Publix without buying a single thing. I got in my car. I put my hands on the steering wheel. I sat there in the parking lot with my hands on the wheel and the air conditioning off and the August sun coming through the windshield, and I tried to remember her name.

It didn't come.

I sat there for 10 minutes.

It still didn't come.

I drove home, and I made it almost to my driveway, and I had to pull over on Heyward Street because I was crying.

Her name was Linda Coker.

I remembered it 3 days later, on a Saturday morning, while I was watering the ferns on the front porch. Just like that. The name fell into my head out of the air. Linda Coker, the head of the special education department at Carver Elementary, who I had worked with for 11 years, who had organized my retirement luncheon in 2019, who had given me a framed photograph of all the teachers signed on the matte that's hanging in my office right now.

Linda Coker.

I sat down on the porch step with the watering can in my hand and I cried again, but this time for a different reason. Relief, partly. Shame, mostly.

Because Linda's name should not have taken 3 days.

I'm Patricia Whitman. I'm 63 years old. I was the principal at Carver Elementary School in Columbia, South Carolina, for 17 years before I retired in 2019. I have a master's degree from the University of South Carolina. I have served on the boards of 2 different community education non-profits. I gave a 25 minute keynote address at a state principals' conference in 2014 without any notes. My memory has been a piece of professional equipment for my entire adult life, and the equipment is starting to fail.

I want to tell you something I have not told my husband or my sister or my best friend Marjorie, which is that the Publix wasn't the first time. It was the time I couldn't deny anymore. But it wasn't the first.

A month before the Publix, I'd been at a doctor's appointment and the front desk woman asked me my date of birth and there was a half second where I could not retrieve it. Half a second. Long enough to feel it but not long enough that the woman noticed. I told her my birthday and she typed it in and the appointment went on.

Two weeks before the Publix, I'd been telling my husband Ed a story about something that had happened at the bank, and I forgot the word for the form they make you sign. Just the regular form. I sat there in my own kitchen looking at my own husband and said, "And so I had to sign the, the, you know, the thing with the lines." The word "deposit slip" came back to me about a minute later. Ed didn't say anything. He didn't make a thing of it. He just nodded along like nothing had happened.

It's the little things that scare you the most. The big things you can pretend are flukes. The little things tell you the truth.

I made myself a list one night about a week after the Publix.

I sat at my desk in the room that used to be my home office and I wrote down every time in the previous 6 months I could remember something not coming when it was supposed to. I wrote down 23 incidents. 23 in 6 months. The day I forgot the gas station was on the right instead of the left. The afternoon I called my niece Susan by my sister's name. The morning I couldn't think of the word for the spice that goes in pumpkin pie until I'd been standing in front of the spice rack for 4 minutes. Nutmeg. Of course nutmeg.

23 incidents that I could remember.

I sat at my desk with my list and I thought, "Patricia, this is the thing you don't want to think about."

My mother had developed dementia in her 70s. I had watched it happen. I had been in the assisted living facility the day she'd called me Margaret, which was her sister's name, who had been dead for 22 years at that point. I had held her hand and said, "Mom. I'm Patricia. I'm your daughter." And she had looked at me with those wide bright eyes and said, "Of course, sweetheart," in the way she said it when she was just going along with what I was telling her without knowing it.

I'd told myself I was going to do everything I could not to be her at the end.

And here I was, 63 years old, with 23 incidents on a piece of paper in front of me.

I called my doctor's office the next morning. I told the woman on the phone that I wanted to talk to Dr. Mehta about memory concerns. She put me down for 3 weeks out.

The 3 weeks felt like 3 years.

In those 3 weeks I read.

I want to tell you what I read because the reading is what changed my life. I want to be clear about something first. I am not telling you reading saved me from dementia. I am not telling you anything will or won't save you from dementia. I am not a doctor and I do not know what your future or my future holds. What I am telling you is what I learned about my brain in those 3 weeks, that nobody had ever sat me down and explained, and what I started doing about it.

The first thing I learned was that the brain is the single most energy hungry organ in the body. By a wide margin. Your brain is about 2 percent of your body weight and it uses about 20 percent of your daily energy. It is a furnace.

And the energy that powers that furnace is produced by little structures inside every brain cell called mitochondria.

I had not thought about mitochondria since 11th grade biology. I went and read about them like I was studying for a test. Mitochondria produce the energy that runs every cell in your body, but they're especially critical to brain cells. Your neurons fire constantly. They are working all day, every day. They need a constant, reliable, clean supply of energy. And the structures that produce that energy take damage over time. The byproducts of normal energy production create a kind of oxidative stress, and that stress accumulates inside the mitochondria year after year. Researchers have a name for the result. They call it mitochondrial dysfunction.

And one of the most studied areas in neuroscience right now is the connection between mitochondrial dysfunction and exactly the kind of slow, frustrating, scary cognitive changes I had been writing on my list.

The forgotten names. The lost words. The half second pauses.

It's not always dementia. Sometimes it is, and sometimes it isn't. But the underlying mechanism, the mitochondrial side of it, is something researchers are taking very seriously, and the reason is that when you understand the mechanism you start to see the openings. You start to see the places where the body might be supported in doing what it's been doing all along. You start to see that "this is just aging" is not the only story available.

I read deeper. I read for hours every night that month. Ed would come in and ask if I was coming to bed and I'd say give me 20 more minutes, and 90 minutes later I'd still be at the desk with the lamp on.

The thing that kept coming up was a compound called urolithin A.

Urolithin A is something your body produces when your gut bacteria break down certain dietary polyphenols. The richest source of the precursors that get converted into urolithin A is pomegranate. Specifically the concentrated polyphenols in the peel and the rind.

And the reason urolithin A has gotten so much research attention recently, including a 2024 study out of the University of Copenhagen that I want to be careful with because the research is still developing and a lot of it is still preclinical, is that urolithin A appears to support a process called mitophagy. Mitophagy is the body's own housekeeping system for clearing out damaged mitochondria so that newer, healthier ones can take their place. It's a process the body has been running for as long as you've been alive. And when it's running well, the cells, including the brain cells, have access to cleaner energy.

When researchers have looked at urolithin A specifically in the context of brain mitochondria, the early signals have been interesting enough that they're now planning clinical trials in humans with cognitive issues.

I want to say it again. I am not telling you this is a cure for anything. I am not a doctor. The research is still developing. What I'm telling you is that there is a mechanism being studied that addresses a real biological process that I, at 63 years old, have likely been losing ground on for the last 20 years.

I read about pomegranate research in other areas too. There have been studies on pomegranate extract and memory. A small double-blind study of middle aged and older adults showed improved verbal and visual memory after 4 weeks of pomegranate juice. A trial at UCLA in adults aged 50 to 75 looking at pomegranate extract found positive signals in cognitive performance at multiple checkpoints. A 2024 trial in 80 individuals dealing with mild cognitive concerns found significantly better outcomes with pomegranate seed oil supplementation alongside a Mediterranean diet compared to diet alone, across global cognition, verbal episodic memory, and processing and executive functions.

I sat at my desk and I read all of this and I thought about Linda Coker.

I thought about my mother.

I thought about the form at the bank.

I thought about 23 incidents in 6 months on a piece of paper.

And I ordered a bottle of Auniva.

Auniva Pomegranate. 2 capsules a day. Made in the US. The concentrated extract from the peel where the active compounds are most highly concentrated. 30 servings per bottle. A 90 day money back guarantee, which I noticed and which mattered to me because at 63 years old I am tired of giving companies my money for products they don't stand behind.

I went to the doctor 9 days after I ordered the bottle. I had the bottle in my purse.

Dr. Mehta is a thoughtful woman. She listened to me for almost 25 minutes. I told her about the Publix. I told her about the list. I told her about my mother. She gave me a cognitive screening test in the office that day, the kind they give you to establish a baseline. She said my results were normal for my age and education. She told me to come back in 6 months and we'd do it again.

She did not dismiss me. I want to be clear about that. She took me seriously. She just also told me that what I was describing was within the range of normal age related cognitive change, and that there was nothing she could prescribe at this point.

I asked her what she thought about pomegranate extract.

She paused. She said, "Patricia, there's some interesting early research. It's not at the level where I would prescribe it. But as a supplement, I don't have any concerns about it. Make sure your supplements and your medications don't conflict and let me know what you're taking."

I told her about the Auniva.

She wrote it in my chart.

I started taking it the next morning.

I want to tell you about the last 4 months because the last 4 months are why I'm writing this.

The first 3 weeks I didn't notice much. I want to say that honestly. I think I was looking too hard. I'd find myself, in the middle of a sentence, asking myself "did that come faster than it would have a month ago." And the answer was usually I don't know. The brain is bad at noticing what it's doing.

Around week 5, something else started happening that I want to tell you about because it surprised me.

I was sleeping better.

I hadn't realized I was sleeping badly until I was sleeping better. Ed and I had been having those middle of the night moments where one of us would be awake at 3 AM and the other would notice and we'd both end up reading on our phones for an hour. They had become so normal we'd stopped commenting on them. Around week 5 I noticed I'd slept through, 4 nights in a row.

By week 7, I noticed I was reading more.

I had been a 4 books a year reader for the last 3 years, which was a disgrace for a person who had run a school for 17 years. I would pick up a book and read 6 pages and lose interest. I started a book in late September and finished it 9 days later. Then I started another one. By the end of November I'd finished 4 books, which used to be my pace in college.

By week 10, I was teaching a Sunday school class for adults.

I want to be careful, again. I don't know what's causing what. I'm not telling you the pomegranate is doing all of it. I'm telling you that 4 months ago I was a woman who left her cart at the Publix and sat in her car crying, and as of last Sunday I stood in front of 22 adults at First Presbyterian and taught for 50 minutes from notes I had largely committed to memory, and I did not lose a single word, a single name, or a single thread.

Yesterday morning I ran into Linda Coker again.

This time it was at the Earth Fare on Devine Street. She was coming out of the coffee bar with a paper cup. She saw me at the same time I saw her.

I said, "Linda. Hello."

Her name came up out of me as easily as the next breath.

She smiled. She came over. She hugged me. She said, "Patricia, oh my goodness, I've been thinking about you. Did you ever want to get that coffee?"

We sat down at one of the little tables right there in the Earth Fare and we had coffee together for 35 minutes. I asked about her daughter at Clemson, by name, because her daughter's name is Caroline. I asked about her husband Tom, by name, because that is also a name I am supposed to know. I talked about my own grandchildren. I told her about Ed's retirement project of restoring a 1972 Mustang. I told her about the Sunday school class. She told me I looked great. She said, "You look like you again, Patricia."

I drove home from Earth Fare and I sat in the driveway for a minute with the car off. I thought about the Publix. I thought about the 10 minutes I'd spent in this exact same car trying to summon a name that wouldn't come, in this exact same driveway with the exact same August sun coming through the exact same windshield.

I sat there and I felt, for the first time in a very long time, like the woman I had been was not gone. She had just been buried under a kind of fog I didn't have a name for, and the fog was lifting. Some of it because I was paying attention. Some of it because I was sleeping. Some of it, I believe, because the brain in my head was finally getting a piece of support it had been quietly asking for for years.

If any of this sounds like the woman you are or the husband or the mother or the friend you love, I'd just say take a look at it.

Auniva Pomegranate is 2 capsules a day, made in the USA, with the concentrated extract from the peel of the fruit where the actual compounds that matter actually live. It comes with a 90 day money back guarantee. You try it for up to 90 days, and if it's not the right fit for you, you ship the bottle back and they refund every penny.

That guarantee is part of why I ordered it. I was tired of buying things that came with no exits. The guarantee told me the company believed in what they were doing. And the way I felt at the Earth Fare with Linda Coker yesterday told me they were right to.

I think about my mother more often these days. I think about her face when she called me Margaret. I think about how much of her had been quietly slipping away from her for years before anybody had a word for what was happening.

I am not going to be her at the end.

I am not telling you that with pride. I am telling you with the kind of careful, quiet hope that comes from being a 63 year old woman who has, for 4 months now, had her words again. Her names again. Her sleep again. Her books again. Her Sunday school class again.

I had been losing pieces of myself in small increments without knowing it.

I am getting some of them back.

The name Linda Coker came up out of me as easily as the next breath.

That is not a miracle. It is something the body has been doing all along, and it just needed a little support to do it again.

She started taking it in November. Last week she called me and said she'd remembered the title of a book she'd been trying to remember for 8 months. It came to her in the shower. She had stood in the shower with the water running and she had cried. We are both at an age where we cry about things like that, and we are not embarrassed about it.
