I listened to my dead husband's voicemail for the 47th time this morning while I sat in my car in the Kroger parking lot with the engine off.

"Hey Janie, it's me, traffic's a mess on 64, I'm gonna be late, don't hold dinner, love you, bye."

11 seconds long. 11 seconds. I have it memorized down to the breath he takes between "love you" and "bye." There's a tiny pause there, like he was about to say something else and didn't. I've spent two years wondering what he was about to say.

Frank died on October 11th, 2023. Massive heart attack at his desk at the Charleston Gazette-Mail, where he'd been a sports editor for 31 years. He was 61. He'd left me that voicemail on April 3rd of that same year. Six months and 8 days before.

I save it. I move it from one phone to the next. The Verizon guy who set up my new iPhone last December asked me if I needed help transferring anything and I said yes, my voicemails, all of them, and he looked at me funny because nobody saves voicemails anymore, but he did it, and I gave him a $20 tip because he didn't ask why.

My name is Janet. Everyone calls me Janie. I'm 58 years old. I live in a brick split-level on the south end of Charleston, West Virginia, the kind of street where the dogwoods come in pink along both curbs in April and where everyone knows whose Subaru is whose. Frank and I bought the house in 1997 when our son Eli was 4. Eli is 33 now, lives in Pittsburgh, calls me every Sunday at 6:30 PM whether I pick up or not.

I haven't checked my blood pressure since the funeral.

I have one of those little arm cuffs in the linen closet, on the second shelf, behind the towels Frank's mother gave us in 1995. It still has the receipt taped to the side because Frank refused to throw away the receipt on anything that cost more than $40. The cuff was $52 from CVS. He bought it after his cardiologist Dr. Marsh told him he needed to start tracking his numbers at home, and Frank, being Frank, came home with one for each of us, because he said if we were going to do something we were going to do it together.

He took his every morning at 6:14 AM, sitting at the kitchen table in his blue plaid robe, before the coffee was even done. He wrote the numbers in a yellow legal pad with the date and a little notation if he'd slept bad or eaten something salty. The legal pad is still in the kitchen drawer. I haven't opened it. I can't.

I haven't taken mine since the morning of October 12th, 2023. Which was the morning after Frank died. I sat at the table by myself and put the cuff on and watched the number come up and then I took the whole machine and put it in the linen closet behind the towels and I haven't touched it since.

The number was 168 over 102, if you're wondering.

I am not stupid. I know what 168 over 102 means. I worked as the office manager at a pediatric practice for 24 years before I retired in 2022. I sat across the desk from Dr. Rinaldi for nearly a quarter century, and I know what a blood pressure reading is supposed to look like, and I know what one looks like when it isn't.

But I also know what grief is. And grief, the kind that comes for a woman who lost her husband suddenly at 61 with no warning, is the kind that says: I will deal with my body later. I will get through Thanksgiving first. I will get through Christmas. I will get through his birthday. I will get through our anniversary. I will get through the one year mark. I will get through the two year mark.

And the years go by and you don't deal with it.

And every morning you wake up and your head feels heavy and your face feels hot when you stand up too fast and you tell yourself it's because you didn't sleep well, or because you're dehydrated, or because the weather changed, or because you had two glasses of wine with Carol on Thursday night. You tell yourself anything except the thing.

The thing is, my husband died of his heart at 61. And I am a 58-year-old woman whose blood pressure was 168 over 102 the morning after he died and who has not checked it in two years and three months.

Carol Whitfield has been my best friend since 1996. She lives 4 streets over on Ridgeway Drive in a yellow Cape Cod with a flagstone path. She and her husband Dr. Marsh, the same Dr. Marsh who'd been Frank's cardiologist, used to come over for cards every other Friday. Dr. Marsh is 64 now, retired in 2024 from his practice but still consults two days a week at CAMC. He was the one who pronounced Frank at the hospital. He drove me home in his own car. He sat at my kitchen table at 9:47 PM that night and didn't say anything for 23 minutes, just sat there with his hand on my hand, and then he said, "Janie, the man loved you to pieces. He talked about you like a boy."

I haven't been able to look him in the eye since.

Not because of anything he did. Because of what he knows.

He knows Frank's numbers. He has them in a file somewhere. He knows what Frank's blood pressure was running in those last 6 months. He knows what mine was the only time I let him take it, at Carol's 55th birthday party in 2022, when he had one of those wrist cuffs out and was making people guess theirs as a joke. Mine was 154 over 96 with a glass of pinot grigio in my hand. He'd raised an eyebrow at me. Said, "Janie, when are you coming in?" I'd laughed and walked into the kitchen for more cheese.

A year and a half later he was driving me home from the hospital where my husband had died.

He has tried to talk to me three times in the last two years. At Frank's memorial. At Eli's wedding in May of 2024. Standing in line at the deli counter at Capitol Market last September. Each time I have made my voice bright and said "I am doing fine, doctor, you take care now," and walked away.

Last Thursday he showed up at my front door at 4:47 PM with a Pyrex casserole dish covered in tinfoil.

Carol was at her sister's in Roanoke. He was alone. He had the casserole in both hands and a folder under his arm.

I stared at him through the storm door for a long second.

"Carol made too much lasagna," he said. "She said you'd take the leftovers off our hands if I begged."

That is a lie. Carol does not over-make lasagna. Carol portions everything in advance because she ran the church food pantry for 11 years. Dr. Marsh knew I knew it was a lie. He held the casserole up a little higher and said, "Can I come in, Janie."

I let him in.

He set the lasagna on the kitchen counter, on the exact spot where Frank used to set the mail on Tuesdays. Then he sat down at the kitchen table without being asked, in Frank's chair, and put his hands flat on the placemat, and looked at me, and said:

"Janie, you haven't been in to see anyone in two years. I know because I have a friend at every cardiology practice in Charleston and I asked. I'm not here as your doctor. I'm here as Frank's friend. And I cannot watch this happen twice."

I didn't say anything.

He opened the folder.

In it was a single piece of paper. A photocopy of Frank's last in-office blood pressure reading from August 14th, 2023. 8 weeks before he died.

158 over 96. With a little note in Dr. Marsh's handwriting in the margin: "FU 3 mo. discuss adjustment."

He never made it to the follow-up.

Dr. Marsh slid the paper across the table toward me. Then he said, very quietly: "Janie, what's yours running."

And I started to cry. Not the polite cry I'd done at the funeral. The other kind. The kind that comes up out of your stomach. I cried in Frank's kitchen for what felt like an hour but was probably 4 minutes. Dr. Marsh didn't move. He didn't reach for me. He just sat there and let me do it.

When I stopped, he said: "Go get the cuff."

I got the cuff. I took it out of the linen closet behind the towels. The receipt was still taped to the side, faded now. I brought it to the kitchen and I sat down across from him at the table and he wrapped it around my arm himself, gently, the way he must have wrapped it around hundreds of women's arms over 34 years of practice, and he pushed the button.

The number came up.

171 over 104.

We sat there looking at it.

He didn't tell me what to do. He didn't lecture me. He didn't write a prescription. He said, "Janie, I want to tell you something I've been telling a handful of people the last 14 months. I would have told Frank if I'd known then what I know now. Will you let me say it."

I nodded.

He sat back in Frank's chair. He told me he'd retired in part because he'd gotten tired of telling 60-year-old men what their wives were going to find when they came home from the hospital that night, and he'd started reading. Reading on his own time. About what actually happens inside a blood vessel when the pressure stays high for years.

He said the inside of your blood vessels has a thin living wall. Just one cell layer thick. He called it the endothelium but he said I could just think of it as the inside lining. He said that lining is the part that decides whether your blood vessels open up or stay tight. It produces a molecule called nitric oxide, and the nitric oxide is what tells the vessel walls to relax.

He said years of inflammation and stress and processed food and grief and not sleeping right wear that lining down. He said when the lining isn't healthy, it can't produce as much nitric oxide. The vessels stay tight. The blood forces its way through. The pressure goes up. And the higher the pressure goes, the more it punishes the lining, which produces even less nitric oxide. A cycle that feeds itself.

He said the medications he'd prescribed Frank, and the ones he would have prescribed me if I'd come in, work by forcing the vessels open. He said they do not touch the lining. He said the lining keeps deteriorating underneath, and the dose goes up over time, and that's why people end up on three medications instead of one, and four instead of three. He said that was the conversation he'd been about to have with Frank at the follow-up Frank never made.

He said he'd been looking for something that helped support the lining itself. He said his daughter, who is a nutritionist in Asheville, sent him an article about a fruit called amla. He said the article was good. He said he read the original studies. He said the science is real, and the mechanism makes sense, and the studies aren't perfect, but he's been taking it himself for 11 months.

He said he'd brought a bottle with him. In the folder, under the photocopy.

It was a small bottle with a green label. Said Auniva on it.

He didn't push it across the table. He just left it next to the photocopy of Frank's last reading and said: "I'm not selling you anything. I don't get a cent. I'm telling you what I'm taking and why."

Then he said the thing that broke me a second time.

He said: "Frank would have taken it, Janie. If he'd known. He was that kind of man. He would have read the same articles I read and he would have ordered a bottle for both of you. You both would have been on it for two years by now."

I looked at the bottle on the table next to the paper that said 158 over 96.

I think you can guess what I did.

I want to slow down here and tell you what I learned in the next 4 days, because I think it matters.

I am not a woman who buys things from Facebook. I am not a woman who falls for things. I worked the front desk at a pediatric practice for 24 years and I have heard every miracle pitch you can imagine from every essential-oil-pyramid-scheme cousin in the state of West Virginia. I am suspicious by trade.

So I read for 4 days before I took the first capsule.

Here's what I figured out, as a 58-year-old woman with no medical degree but a quarter century of sitting next to a doctor at lunch.

Your blood pressure is not a separate problem from the rest of your body. It is a downstream signal of what is happening on the inside of your blood vessels. The inside lining. The endothelium. When that lining is functioning the way it did when you were 30, it produces nitric oxide. Your vessels relax. Your blood flows easily. Your pressure stays where it should.

When the lining is worn down, the lining produces less nitric oxide. Your vessels stay tight. Your heart has to push harder. The number on the cuff goes up.

Pills can lower the number. Pills cannot heal the lining.

What amla appears to do is different. It contains compounds called emblicanins that help support that inner lining. When the lining is supported, it can start producing more of its own nitric oxide, the way it did when you were younger. Vessels can relax more naturally. Blood flows more freely. The pressure on the walls can ease. And when the pressure eases, the lining isn't under the same constant beating anymore. The cycle can start to break.

Pressure can come down. Not because something forced it. Because the body is doing what it already knew how to do. The lining just had to be supported first.

That sentence sat in my kitchen with me for a long time the night I read it.

The lining just had to be supported first.

Frank had been on losartan for 6 years. The dose had been raised twice. Two months before he died, Dr. Marsh had wanted to add a second medication. Frank had pushed back. He'd said he wanted to try diet first. He'd been doing the DASH diet for 11 weeks. He'd lost 9 pounds. His pressure had not budged.

Because the diet wasn't reaching the lining. And the pill wasn't reaching the lining. Nothing he had ever taken or eaten in 6 years had reached the lining.

I ordered a bottle that Thursday night. From the website Dr. Marsh wrote down on the back of the photocopy. auniva.co/amla/33. He told me to use that link because it had something to do with their guarantee. 90 days. If it doesn't work, you send the bottle back and they refund you. Every penny.

I want to say something about that guarantee. Because I'm 58 and I have been around long enough to know that a real money-back guarantee is rare. The losartan Frank took for 6 years did not come with one. The DASH diet book on his nightstand did not come with one. The wrist cuff at Carol's birthday party did not come with one. Nothing about his hypertension treatment, in 6 years of treatment, came with a refund if it failed.

It failed. Nobody offered Frank his time back. Nobody offered me my husband back.

Auniva offers you 90 days. You take it for 90 days. If your pressure doesn't move, you send the bottle back and they refund you. That is more than fair to a woman who has been burned before.

The bottle arrived on Tuesday.

I took the first two capsules with my eggs Wednesday morning. November 27th. The morning before Thanksgiving.

Eli came home for Thanksgiving. He noticed I'd cried. He didn't ask why. He hugged me longer than usual at the door and said, "Mom, you look tired." I said, "I know."

I started taking the cuff out of the linen closet every morning at 6:14 AM. Frank's time. I sat at the kitchen table in his blue plaid robe, which I'd been wearing since the second week after he died. I wrote the numbers in the yellow legal pad. In the same column where Frank had stopped writing. I started a new page so the handwriting wouldn't confuse me.

Week one: 168/103. 171/104. 169/102. 166/101. 170/103. 165/100. 167/102.

I cried looking at those numbers. Because they were almost identical to the morning after he died.

Week two: 162/99. 164/100. 159/97. 161/98. 158/97. 160/98. 156/96.

Week three: 152/93. 154/94. 149/91. 151/92. 148/90. 150/92. 147/89.

I called Dr. Marsh on the morning of December 18th when the cuff said 144/87 because I thought it might be broken. He laughed for the first time I'd heard him laugh in two years. He said, "Janie, it's not broken."

I am sitting in my kitchen right now, on a Tuesday morning in May, writing this. I took my pressure 47 minutes ago. 128/81. I have not seen a number that low since 2019.

I want to tell you about the other things, because the numbers don't tell the whole story.

I sleep again. I don't mean I sleep more hours. I mean I sleep through the night without waking up at 3:14 AM with my heart in my ears. That had been happening for 17 months. I'd been telling myself it was grief.

The headaches I'd been having since the funeral are gone. I thought those were grief too. They weren't grief. They were 168 over 102 for two years.

I can walk to the end of my driveway and back without my face getting hot. I'd stopped getting the mail myself in October of 2024. I have a neighbor's grandson who'd been doing it for $5 a week.

I called him last Saturday and told him he was fired but I'd still pay him through June.

My son called me last Sunday and said, "Mom, you sound like yourself again."

He didn't know I'd ever stopped sounding like myself.

I haven't listened to the voicemail in 6 weeks. I still have it. I'll always have it. But I don't need to listen to it every morning to remember Frank, because for the first time in two years I'm not punishing myself for surviving him.

If you're reading this and you have a number you've been hiding from, a cuff in a linen closet, a yellow legal pad you can't open, a voicemail you've memorized down to the breath, I want you to hear me.

Frank ran out of time because nobody told him there was anything to do besides the pill. I do not want you to run out of time.

Auniva has a 90 day money-back guarantee. If your numbers don't move, you send the bottle back and they refund you. No phone call. No fight. They refund you. The losartan didn't come with that. Neither did the diet book. Neither did the six years of three-month follow-ups.

This does.

P.S. You'll know it's working before the cuff confirms it. For me it was the headaches. Mine had become so constant I'd stopped noticing them, the way you stop noticing a fan running in another room until somebody turns it off. Week two the room got quiet. I sat at the kitchen table with my coffee and realized I didn't have a headache, and I started crying because I hadn't remembered what it felt like to not have one. If you've been telling yourself the headache is grief, or the heaviness in your chest is grief, or the way your face gets hot when you stand up is grief, please consider that some of it is grief and some of it might be the lining, and there's something you can do about the lining.

P.P.S. About the guarantee. 90 days is unusual. Most companies give you 30. 30 days is barely long enough to know if something's working for a body that has been running on a damaged lining for a decade. Auniva gives you 90. That is three full bottles. That is enough time to see your numbers move on a cuff you've been hiding from. The only reason a company offers a guarantee that long is because they already know what you're going to find out.

P.P.P.S. Dr. Marsh told me Auniva is a small company and they sometimes sell out. He'd had to wait 8 days for his second bottle in February. I keep two in the kitchen drawer now, where Frank's legal pad used to live. One open, one sealed. Because I am not going back to 171 over 104. Not for one morning. Not for one week. Not for anyone.

P.P.P.P.S. If you're a widow, or a wife whose husband won't go to the doctor, or a daughter watching your mother slide the cuff back into the linen closet, please send her this. I am writing it because no one wrote it for me when I needed it. I am writing it because the casserole Dr. Marsh brought over wasn't a casserole, it was a chance, and I almost didn't open the door. Open the door. Open the linen closet. Open the bottle.

Frank would have wanted you to.

body:
I forgot a woman's name at the Publix on Forest Drive and sat in my car for 10 minutes afterward.

It was a Wednesday morning, around 10:30, and I was in the produce section pinching avocados the way my mother taught me to. I had my list in my pocket. I had nowhere to be. I was the most relaxed I'd been all week, and that's the part that's important, because what happened next happened to a relaxed woman in good spirits, which is not the version of me you'd expect to fall apart.

A voice said, "Patricia."

I turned around.

The woman was in her mid 40s. Blonde hair pulled back. Cream colored cardigan. A toddler in the cart who had to be a grandchild, because she was too put together for a young mother and her face had that 40-something softness.

She said my name like we were friends.

She smiled at me the way you smile at somebody you've shared something with. She said, "Oh my goodness, it's been so long. How are you?" And she came around the avocado bin with her arms half open, the way somebody does when they're going in for the hug but they're checking to see if you want one too.

And I stood there with an avocado in my hand and I had absolutely no idea who she was.

I knew I knew her. I knew it deep in some part of me that wasn't connecting to whatever part is supposed to know names. Her face was familiar in a way that made it worse. If she'd been a total stranger I could have just said, "I'm sorry, I think you have me confused with someone else." But I knew her. We had history. And the history was just gone.

I did what you do.

I hugged her. I said, "Oh my goodness, it's been forever. How are you?" I asked about her, generally, in the kind of vague way you can ask without giving anything away. She told me her oldest had gotten into Clemson. I made the appropriate sounds. She told me she'd retired from the district 2 years ago. I felt something cold move down my back, because if she'd been with the district, I had almost certainly known her name as well as I knew the names of my own children.

She talked for about 4 minutes. I nodded. I smiled. I asked about her husband, generically. She told me about her husband, whose name I also did not retrieve. She told me about a vacation they were taking. She said she'd been meaning to call me. She said we should get coffee.

And then she said, "Well, I'll let you finish your shopping. So good to see you, Patricia."

She hugged me again. She wheeled her cart away. The toddler waved at me over her shoulder.

I stood there with the avocado in my hand.

I put it in my cart. I picked up a different one. I put that one in my cart too. I walked over to the bananas. I stood by the bananas for what felt like 2 minutes. My heart was going. My hands had that buzzing feeling you get when you've had too much coffee.

I left my cart there.

I walked out of the Publix without buying a single thing. I got in my car. I put my hands on the steering wheel. I sat there in the parking lot with my hands on the wheel and the air conditioning off and the August sun coming through the windshield, and I tried to remember her name.

It didn't come.

I sat there for 10 minutes.

It still didn't come.

I drove home, and I made it almost to my driveway, and I had to pull over on Heyward Street because I was crying.

Her name was Linda Coker.

I remembered it 3 days later, on a Saturday morning, while I was watering the ferns on the front porch. Just like that. The name fell into my head out of the air. Linda Coker, the head of the special education department at Carver Elementary, who I had worked with for 11 years, who had organized my retirement luncheon in 2019, who had given me a framed photograph of all the teachers signed on the matte that's hanging in my office right now.

Linda Coker.

I sat down on the porch step with the watering can in my hand and I cried again, but this time for a different reason. Relief, partly. Shame, mostly.

Because Linda's name should not have taken 3 days.

I'm Patricia Whitman. I'm 63 years old. I was the principal at Carver Elementary School in Columbia, South Carolina, for 17 years before I retired in 2019. I have a master's degree from the University of South Carolina. I have served on the boards of 2 different community education non-profits. I gave a 25 minute keynote address at a state principals' conference in 2014 without any notes. My memory has been a piece of professional equipment for my entire adult life, and the equipment is starting to fail.

I want to tell you something I have not told my husband or my sister or my best friend Marjorie, which is that the Publix wasn't the first time. It was the time I couldn't deny anymore. But it wasn't the first.

A month before the Publix, I'd been at a doctor's appointment and the front desk woman asked me my date of birth and there was a half second where I could not retrieve it. Half a second. Long enough to feel it but not long enough that the woman noticed. I told her my birthday and she typed it in and the appointment went on.

Two weeks before the Publix, I'd been telling my husband Ed a story about something that had happened at the bank, and I forgot the word for the form they make you sign. Just the regular form. I sat there in my own kitchen looking at my own husband and said, "And so I had to sign the, the, you know, the thing with the lines." The word "deposit slip" came back to me about a minute later. Ed didn't say anything. He didn't make a thing of it. He just nodded along like nothing had happened.

It's the little things that scare you the most. The big things you can pretend are flukes. The little things tell you the truth.

I made myself a list one night about a week after the Publix.

I sat at my desk in the room that used to be my home office and I wrote down every time in the previous 6 months I could remember something not coming when it was supposed to. I wrote down 23 incidents. 23 in 6 months. The day I forgot the gas station was on the right instead of the left. The afternoon I called my niece Susan by my sister's name. The morning I couldn't think of the word for the spice that goes in pumpkin pie until I'd been standing in front of the spice rack for 4 minutes. Nutmeg. Of course nutmeg.

23 incidents that I could remember.

I sat at my desk with my list and I thought, "Patricia, this is the thing you don't want to think about."

My mother had developed dementia in her 70s. I had watched it happen. I had been in the assisted living facility the day she'd called me Margaret, which was her sister's name, who had been dead for 22 years at that point. I had held her hand and said, "Mom. I'm Patricia. I'm your daughter." And she had looked at me with those wide bright eyes and said, "Of course, sweetheart," in the way she said it when she was just going along with what I was telling her without knowing it.

I'd told myself I was going to do everything I could not to be her at the end.

And here I was, 63 years old, with 23 incidents on a piece of paper in front of me.

I called my doctor's office the next morning. I told the woman on the phone that I wanted to talk to Dr. Mehta about memory concerns. She put me down for 3 weeks out.

The 3 weeks felt like 3 years.

In those 3 weeks I read.

I want to tell you what I read because the reading is what changed my life. I want to be clear about something first. I am not telling you reading saved me from dementia. I am not telling you anything will or won't save you from dementia. I am not a doctor and I do not know what your future or my future holds. What I am telling you is what I learned about my brain in those 3 weeks, that nobody had ever sat me down and explained, and what I started doing about it.

The first thing I learned was that the brain is the single most energy hungry organ in the body. By a wide margin. Your brain is about 2 percent of your body weight and it uses about 20 percent of your daily energy. It is a furnace.

And the energy that powers that furnace is produced by little structures inside every brain cell called mitochondria.

I had not thought about mitochondria since 11th grade biology. I went and read about them like I was studying for a test. Mitochondria produce the energy that runs every cell in your body, but they're especially critical to brain cells. Your neurons fire constantly. They are working all day, every day. They need a constant, reliable, clean supply of energy. And the structures that produce that energy take damage over time. The byproducts of normal energy production create a kind of oxidative stress, and that stress accumulates inside the mitochondria year after year. Researchers have a name for the result. They call it mitochondrial dysfunction.

And one of the most studied areas in neuroscience right now is the connection between mitochondrial dysfunction and exactly the kind of slow, frustrating, scary cognitive changes I had been writing on my list.

The forgotten names. The lost words. The half second pauses.

It's not always dementia. Sometimes it is, and sometimes it isn't. But the underlying mechanism, the mitochondrial side of it, is something researchers are taking very seriously, and the reason is that when you understand the mechanism you start to see the openings. You start to see the places where the body might be supported in doing what it's been doing all along. You start to see that "this is just aging" is not the only story available.

I read deeper. I read for hours every night that month. Ed would come in and ask if I was coming to bed and I'd say give me 20 more minutes, and 90 minutes later I'd still be at the desk with the lamp on.

The thing that kept coming up was a compound called urolithin A.

Urolithin A is something your body produces when your gut bacteria break down certain dietary polyphenols. The richest source of the precursors that get converted into urolithin A is pomegranate. Specifically the concentrated polyphenols in the peel and the rind.

And the reason urolithin A has gotten so much research attention recently, including a 2024 study out of the University of Copenhagen that I want to be careful with because the research is still developing and a lot of it is still preclinical, is that urolithin A appears to support a process called mitophagy. Mitophagy is the body's own housekeeping system for clearing out damaged mitochondria so that newer, healthier ones can take their place. It's a process the body has been running for as long as you've been alive. And when it's running well, the cells, including the brain cells, have access to cleaner energy.

When researchers have looked at urolithin A specifically in the context of brain mitochondria, the early signals have been interesting enough that they're now planning clinical trials in humans with cognitive issues.

I want to say it again. I am not telling you this is a cure for anything. I am not a doctor. The research is still developing. What I'm telling you is that there is a mechanism being studied that addresses a real biological process that I, at 63 years old, have likely been losing ground on for the last 20 years.

I read about pomegranate research in other areas too. There have been studies on pomegranate extract and memory. A small double-blind study of middle aged and older adults showed improved verbal and visual memory after 4 weeks of pomegranate juice. A trial at UCLA in adults aged 50 to 75 looking at pomegranate extract found positive signals in cognitive performance at multiple checkpoints. A 2024 trial in 80 individuals dealing with mild cognitive concerns found significantly better outcomes with pomegranate seed oil supplementation alongside a Mediterranean diet compared to diet alone, across global cognition, verbal episodic memory, and processing and executive functions.

I sat at my desk and I read all of this and I thought about Linda Coker.

I thought about my mother.

I thought about the form at the bank.

I thought about 23 incidents in 6 months on a piece of paper.

And I ordered a bottle of Auniva.

Auniva Pomegranate. 2 capsules a day. Made in the US. The concentrated extract from the peel where the active compounds are most highly concentrated. 30 servings per bottle. A 90 day money back guarantee, which I noticed and which mattered to me because at 63 years old I am tired of giving companies my money for products they don't stand behind.

I went to the doctor 9 days after I ordered the bottle. I had the bottle in my purse.

Dr. Mehta is a thoughtful woman. She listened to me for almost 25 minutes. I told her about the Publix. I told her about the list. I told her about my mother. She gave me a cognitive screening test in the office that day, the kind they give you to establish a baseline. She said my results were normal for my age and education. She told me to come back in 6 months and we'd do it again.

She did not dismiss me. I want to be clear about that. She took me seriously. She just also told me that what I was describing was within the range of normal age related cognitive change, and that there was nothing she could prescribe at this point.

I asked her what she thought about pomegranate extract.

She paused. She said, "Patricia, there's some interesting early research. It's not at the level where I would prescribe it. But as a supplement, I don't have any concerns about it. Make sure your supplements and your medications don't conflict and let me know what you're taking."

I told her about the Auniva.

She wrote it in my chart.

I started taking it the next morning.

I want to tell you about the last 4 months because the last 4 months are why I'm writing this.

The first 3 weeks I didn't notice much. I want to say that honestly. I think I was looking too hard. I'd find myself, in the middle of a sentence, asking myself "did that come faster than it would have a month ago." And the answer was usually I don't know. The brain is bad at noticing what it's doing.

Around week 5, something else started happening that I want to tell you about because it surprised me.

I was sleeping better.

I hadn't realized I was sleeping badly until I was sleeping better. Ed and I had been having those middle of the night moments where one of us would be awake at 3 AM and the other would notice and we'd both end up reading on our phones for an hour. They had become so normal we'd stopped commenting on them. Around week 5 I noticed I'd slept through, 4 nights in a row.

By week 7, I noticed I was reading more.

I had been a 4 books a year reader for the last 3 years, which was a disgrace for a person who had run a school for 17 years. I would pick up a book and read 6 pages and lose interest. I started a book in late September and finished it 9 days later. Then I started another one. By the end of November I'd finished 4 books, which used to be my pace in college.

By week 10, I was teaching a Sunday school class for adults.

I want to be careful, again. I don't know what's causing what. I'm not telling you the pomegranate is doing all of it. I'm telling you that 4 months ago I was a woman who left her cart at the Publix and sat in her car crying, and as of last Sunday I stood in front of 22 adults at First Presbyterian and taught for 50 minutes from notes I had largely committed to memory, and I did not lose a single word, a single name, or a single thread.

Yesterday morning I ran into Linda Coker again.

This time it was at the Earth Fare on Devine Street. She was coming out of the coffee bar with a paper cup. She saw me at the same time I saw her.

I said, "Linda. Hello."

Her name came up out of me as easily as the next breath.

She smiled. She came over. She hugged me. She said, "Patricia, oh my goodness, I've been thinking about you. Did you ever want to get that coffee?"

We sat down at one of the little tables right there in the Earth Fare and we had coffee together for 35 minutes. I asked about her daughter at Clemson, by name, because her daughter's name is Caroline. I asked about her husband Tom, by name, because that is also a name I am supposed to know. I talked about my own grandchildren. I told her about Ed's retirement project of restoring a 1972 Mustang. I told her about the Sunday school class. She told me I looked great. She said, "You look like you again, Patricia."

I drove home from Earth Fare and I sat in the driveway for a minute with the car off. I thought about the Publix. I thought about the 10 minutes I'd spent in this exact same car trying to summon a name that wouldn't come, in this exact same driveway with the exact same August sun coming through the exact same windshield.

I sat there and I felt, for the first time in a very long time, like the woman I had been was not gone. She had just been buried under a kind of fog I didn't have a name for, and the fog was lifting. Some of it because I was paying attention. Some of it because I was sleeping. Some of it, I believe, because the brain in my head was finally getting a piece of support it had been quietly asking for for years.

If any of this sounds like the woman you are or the husband or the mother or the friend you love, I'd just say take a look at it.

Auniva Pomegranate is 2 capsules a day, made in the USA, with the concentrated extract from the peel of the fruit where the actual compounds that matter actually live. It comes with a 90 day money back guarantee. You try it for up to 90 days, and if it's not the right fit for you, you ship the bottle back and they refund every penny.

That guarantee is part of why I ordered it. I was tired of buying things that came with no exits. The guarantee told me the company believed in what they were doing. And the way I felt at the Earth Fare with Linda Coker yesterday told me they were right to.

I think about my mother more often these days. I think about her face when she called me Margaret. I think about how much of her had been quietly slipping away from her for years before anybody had a word for what was happening.

I am not going to be her at the end.

I am not telling you that with pride. I am telling you with the kind of careful, quiet hope that comes from being a 63 year old woman who has, for 4 months now, had her words again. Her names again. Her sleep again. Her books again. Her Sunday school class again.

I had been losing pieces of myself in small increments without knowing it.

I am getting some of them back.

The name Linda Coker came up out of me as easily as the next breath.

That is not a miracle. It is something the body has been doing all along, and it just needed a little support to do it again.

P.S. I told my best friend Marjorie about Auniva about 6 weeks after I started. Marjorie is 62 and a retired social worker. She had been having her own version of what I'd been having. She started taking it in November. Last week she called me and said she'd remembered the title of a book she'd been trying to remember for 8 months. It came to her in the shower. She had stood in the shower with the water running and she had cried. We are both at an age where we cry about things like that, and we are not embarrassed about it.

P.P.S. About the 90 day money back guarantee. It's real. If you give Auniva Pomegranate an honest try for up to 90 days and it's not the right fit for you, you ship the bottle back to them and they refund every penny. There's no fight. There's no fine print I've been able to find that contradicts it, and I am a retired school principal who reads things carefully. Most of what doctors and pharmacies hand out doesn't come with any guarantee at all. Auniva stands behind theirs, which says something to me about a company. It should say something to you too.

P.P.P.S. The thing I would say to anyone reading this who has been making lists like the one I made is don't wait. I waited 4 years before I made my list. I had been losing ground for at least that long, and probably longer, before the Publix forced me to admit it. The brain doesn't wait for you to be ready. The brain keeps doing what it's doing whether you're paying attention to it or not. Pay attention now. Today is a better day than the day you walk out of a grocery store without your cart.

P.P.P.P.S. Ed has been taking it too for about 2 months. He hasn't said much about it. He's not a man who says much. But last Thursday at dinner he said, "Patty. I was looking for my reading glasses for 20 minutes this afternoon and then I remembered I'd left them in the garage. I haven't been able to do that in 3 years." He kept eating his pork chop. He didn't make a thing of it. I sat across the table from him and I made a thing of it inside my chest where he couldn't see, and I held on to that little sentence the way you hold on to a small bird that's flown into the house. Gently. Carefully. Hoping it will stay.

A dream is a field of wild buckwheat, steeped in frost under the moonlight; you are the one walking toward it, traversing earthen slopes and following the fine, distinct ridges along the edges of the leaves. As long as the buckwheat remains, your direction holds true.

The journey of chasing a dream is like walking toward that wild buckwheat field on a moonlit late-autumn night. There are moments of hesitation when fallen leaves obscure the slope and the path ahead is unclear; moments of quiet stillness when rising mist blends the buckwheat into the surrounding grasses, making it hard to distinguish; and moments when the wind stirs again, allowing you to trace the fine ridges on the leaf edges and confirm you are still on the right track. It is this interplay of tactile sensation and the surrounding darkness that transforms you—from someone eager to rush into the field—into a night-traveler who trusts that the wild buckwheat, marked by those ridged edges, is waiting for you in the moonlight. 💪🌙 Whenever the wind falls silent and the buckwheat’s silhouette blurs in the mist, you pause to gently stroke the edge of a leaf—its margin lined with fine, distinct ridges that are sharper and more defined than the surrounding wild grass, feeling like a row of microscopic saw-teeth that prick the skin ever so slightly. By following the sensation of those ridges through the darkness, you will find that field of wild buckwheat.

One day, you will cross the final slope and find the buckwheat field right before you; moonlight will bathe the tiny white blossoms, and the ridged leaf edges will cast intricate shadows in the glow. You will crouch down, pluck a leaf, and let your fingertips glide along its edge, feeling the texture of those fine ridges against your skin. Looking back at the slopes you traversed through the dark, guided by those ridges, you will find peace in embracing the self who—even when the buckwheat’s outline was repeatedly swallowed by the night—kept walking, guided all the way by the ridges on the leaves. 🍂🌙 The most moving moment isn't when moonlight falls upon the leaves, but rather the way—even when the buckwheat remains unseen—you trust that the fine, ridged edges brushing against your fingertips are leading you toward that field of wild buckwheat ahead. Every leaf swallowed by the darkness returns to your touch the moment you arrive.

🌙 No darkness is deeper than a field of wild buckwheat defined by the ridges along its leaf edges; no earthen slope is too long for someone willing to trace those edges and feel their fine texture in the night. Even if the buckwheat’s silhouette has completely merged with the dark, keep walking along the slope. The ridges on the leaves will guide you; when you reach the edge of the field, the moonlight will perfectly illuminate the leaf—with its finely textured edges—resting in your hand.

Do not stop simply because you cannot see; reach out, search, and find your own moonlit field of wild buckwheat. 💥🌍 Even the longest slope can be traversed one step at a time. Press on—the ridged edges of the leaves are waiting for you up ahead. 🙌👇
